h: When Optics is not the right tool
d: Learn what Optics does, what it tests, and the fastest way to see it run.
x: Optics is open-source test automation for apps on Android, iOS, the web, TV and the desktop. You describe what a person does in your app, such as signing in or adding a product to the cart. Optics repeats it on a real device, an emulator or a browser, and tells you when the app stops behaving. How a test works # A test is a short list of steps in a file, one action per row. A step reads like a sentence: Press Element Sign in , Enter Text email field ava@birch.shop . You don't write code to find things on screen. Optics looks for each element several ways, cheapest first: by its position in the app's UI tree, by its visible text, by reading a screenshot, and by matching a picture of it. When a redesign breaks one way, the next one takes over, so tests break less often. When a run finishes, you get a pass or fail for every step, screenshots of what Optics saw, and a JUnit report that any CI system can read. What you can test # Target How Optics drives it Android and iOS apps Through Appium , on emulators, simulators and real phones Websites Through Playwright or Selenium , no device needed Android TV, Samsung Tizen, LG webOS Through Appium, with the remote's arrow keys. See TV macOS, Linux and Windows desktop apps Through Appium and the accessibility tree of the OS. See Desktop Locked-down production devices As a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, with a camera watching the screen. See Production devices Optics runs on macOS, Linux and Windows with Python 3.12 or newer. There is no account, cloud service or API key. Everything runs on your machine or in your CI. When Optics is not the right tool # Optics tests what a person does through the interface. Reach for something else for unit tests, load testing, API-only contract tests, or pixel-by-pixel visual comparison. d: Install the optics command, then add only the drivers and engines your platform needs.
x: Optics has two parts. The core is the optics command, which reads your tests and runs them. Engines are optional add-ons: a driver for each kind of target (browser, phone, TV) and extra ways to find things on screen. You install the core once and add engines as you need them. Before you begin # You need Python 3.12 or newer . Check with: $ python3 --version Python 3.12.13 If you have an older version, install a current one from python.org or your system's package manager. Install the core # We recommend the installer. It creates a private Python environment under ~/.optics , adds optics to your PATH, and leaves your system Python alone. $ curl -fsSL https://optics-framework.org/install | sh PS> irm https://optics-framework.org/install.ps1 | iex Use pip when you manage your own virtual environment, for example inside a CI job or an existing test repository. $ python3 -m venv .venv $ source .venv/bin/activate $ pip install optics-framework Open a new terminal so it picks up the updated PATH, then check the install: $ optics --version Optics Framework 1.11.4 Installer options Pass options after sh -s -- . On Windows, set the matching environment variable before running the installer. Option Windows variable What it does --version 1.11.4 OPTICS_VERSION Install a specific release. --extra appium,easyocr OPTICS_EXTRA Install engines at the same time. --dir PATH OPTICS_INSTALL_DIR Install somewhere other than ~/.optics . --no-modify-path OPTICS_NO_MODIFY_PATH Don't edit your shell profile. --dry-run Print what would happen and change nothing. --uninstall Remove Optics and the PATH entry it added. $ curl -fsSL https://optics-framework.org/install | sh -s -- --extra playwright,easyocr Add engines for your platform # The core install ships without drivers, so it stays small. Add the ones for what you test. optics setup installs engines that match your Optics version: $ optics setup --install playwright Playwright needs no server. Optics downloads its Chromium browser for you. To use Selenium instead, see Web . $ optics setup --install appium You also need the Appium server, the Android SDK (for adb ) and a device or emulator. Set up Android testing covers each one. $ optics setup --install appium You also need the Appium server with the XCUITest driver, Xcode, and a simulator or device. See iOS . $ optics setup --install appium You also need Appium and appium-xa11y-driver on the computer that shows the app. One setup script installs both. See Set up the Host . Run optics setup with no options to pick engines from a list instead, or optics setup --list to see every name. Optional engines # Add these when a page tells you to. You don't need them for your first test. Engine Install name Adds EasyOCR easyocr Finds elements by reading text on a screenshot. Runs locally. Tesseract pytesseract A lighter OCR engine. Needs the Tesseract program installed too. Google Vision google-vision Cloud OCR. Needs Google Cloud credentials. AI model gemini , openai or anthropic Plain-English test creation and AI self-heal. Pick the one for your account; see Describe it . MCP server mcp Lets AI agents drive Optics. The installer always includes it; with pip: pip install "optics-framework[mcp]" . Bundles install several at once: mobile (Appium), web (Playwright and Selenium), vision (all OCR engines), llm (all three AI engines) and all (everything except the MCP server). The engines reference lists every engine. Check your setup # optics doctor checks Python, each engine, and the tools around them: $ optics doctor 🩺 optics doctor Core ✅ python 3.12.13 ✅ optics-framework installed, version 1.11.4 Engines ⚠️ Appium appium-python-client not installed → optics setup --install appium ✅ Playwright playwright 1.63.0 Web ✅ playwright browser Chromium download found ✅ rows are ready. ⚠️ rows are optional or not needed for your platform. Pass a project folder ( optics doctor my_project ) to also check its config.yaml . If the install doesn't work # ** optics: command

d: Build a test from scratch that signs in to an online store and adds a product to the cart.
x: You'll write a complete test by hand: open a store, sign in, add a backpack to the cart, and check that it worked. Along the way you'll meet the four files every Optics project uses, and see what happens when a test fails. The test runs in a browser against Sauce Labs' demo store , a public site built for practising test automation. You don't need a phone, an emulator or an account. Before you begin Install Optics and the Playwright engine. If you ran the quickstart , you already have both. $ optics setup --install playwright 1 Create an empty project # $ optics init first-test Optics asks which template to start from. Type 1 for (Blank project) and press Enter. You get a folder with empty files and headers already in place: first-test/ ├── config.yaml ├── test_cases/test_cases.csv ├── modules/modules.csv └── test_data/elements.csv The folder names are only a convention. Optics recognises each file by the column names in its first row, so you can move files around later. 2 Tell Optics to use a browser # config.yaml says what Optics drives. Replace its contents with this: config.yaml driver_sources : - playwright : enabled : true elements_sources : - playwright_find_element : enabled : true - playwright_page_source : enabled : true - playwright_screenshot : enabled : true log_level : WARNING driver_sources picks the browser driver. elements_sources lists the ways Optics may look at the page: asking the browser directly, reading the page's HTML, and taking screenshots. log_level: WARNING keeps the terminal quiet so you can read the results. 3 Name the things you'll touch # Before writing steps, give each field and button a name. Open test_data/elements.csv and add four rows under the header: test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID username_field , //input[@id='user-name'] password_field , //input[@id='password'] login_button , //input[@id='login-button'] backpack_add_button , //button[@id='add-to-cart-sauce-labs-backpack'] The left column is the name you'll use in steps. The right column tells Optics how to find it. These are XPaths : paths into the page's structure. //input[@id='user-name'] means "the input whose id is user-name ". Finding an element's id Open the store in Chrome, right-click a field and choose Inspect . The highlighted HTML shows the element's id . You don't always need XPaths: Define elements shows how to use visible text and pictures instead. 4 Write the steps # Steps live in modules : small, reusable groups of actions. Open modules/modules.csv and add three modules: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2 Open the store , Launch App , https://www.saucedemo.com Sign in , Enter Text , ${username_field} , standard_user Sign in , Enter Text , ${password_field} , secret_sauce Sign in , Press Element , ${login_button} Sign in , Assert Presence , Products Add the backpack to the cart , Press Element , ${backpack_add_button} Add the backpack to the cart , Assert Presence , Remove Read each row left to right: the module it belongs to, a keyword (the action), then the values the keyword needs. ${username_field} refers to the name you defined in the previous step. Products and Remove are plain text that should appear on screen: the products page title, and the label the backpack's button changes to once it's in the cart. 5 Turn the modules into a test case # A test case is a named flow made of modules, run in order. Open test_cases/test_cases.csv : test_cases/test_cases.csv test_case,test_step Shopper can add a backpack , Open the store Shopper can add a backpack , Sign in Shopper can add a backpack , Add the backpack to the cart 6 Check the test without running it # optics dry_run reads every file and checks that each keyword exists and each ${name} is defined. It doesn't click anything, so it's a quick way to catch typos: $ optics dry_run first-test Test Suite └── Shopper can add a backpack | 0.00s | PASS ├── Open the store | 0.00s | PASS ├── Sign in | 0.00s | PASS └── Add the backpack to

d: Learn the five ideas every Optics test is built from, and what happens when a test runs.
x: An Optics test is data, not code. You write down what a person does in plain rows. Optics works out how to do each step on the screen in front of it. Keywords # A keyword is one action or check, such as Press Element , Enter Text or Assert Presence . Every step in a test is one keyword plus the values it needs. Keywords fall into four groups: Group Use it to Examples App management Open and close the app or website Launch App , Close And Terminate App Actions Tap, type, swipe and press keys Press Element , Enter Text , Scroll Verification Check what's on screen Assert Presence , Assert Text , Validate Element Flow control Repeat steps, branch, read data, call APIs Run Loop , Condition , Read Data The same keywords work on every platform. Press Element taps on a phone and clicks in a browser. The keyword reference lists all of them, and optics list prints them in your terminal. Elements # An element is a name for something on screen, like sign_in or search_bar . Steps use the name inside ${…} , and elements.csv says how to find it: test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID sign_in , //*[@resource-id='login'] sign_in , Sign in search_bar , //*[@resource-id='search'] Keeping locators in one file means a redesign is a one-line change, not an edit to every test. An element can have several values. sign_in above can be found by its id or by its text, and Optics tries them in order until one works. A value can be an XPath (a path through the app's UI tree), visible text, or the file name of a picture of the element. Elements can also hold plain data, such as a username, so one file holds everything a test might change. Modules # A module is a named, reusable sequence of steps, like Sign In or Add To Cart . Write a flow once as a module and reuse it in as many test cases as you like. When the sign-in screen changes, you fix one module. Test cases # A test case is a flow you want to check, made of modules in order. Checkout might run Sign In , Add To Cart and Pay . Each test case passes or fails on its own. Two names are special. A test case called Suite Setup runs before all the others, and Suite Teardown runs after them. Use them to launch the app once and close it at the end. Configuration # config.yaml says what Optics drives and how it may look at the screen. It holds lists of engines : A driver controls the target: Appium for phones and TVs, Playwright or Selenium for browsers, or a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse for locked-down devices. Element sources are ways to look at the screen: ask the app directly, read its UI tree, or take a screenshot. Text detection (OCR) and image detection are optional. They let Optics find elements on a screenshot when the UI tree can't help. The tests themselves never mention engines. That's why the same test runs on a phone today and against a different device tomorrow. What happens during a run # When you run optics execute , Optics: Reads every file in the project folder and decides what each one is from its column names. Runs Suite Setup , then each test case in order, then Suite Teardown . For each step, takes a screenshot, finds the element, and performs the action. If a step fails, skips the rest of that test case and moves on to the next one. One broken flow doesn't stop the run. At the end, checks the last screen for known error messages, if you've defined any . Writes the results to execution_output/ , and exits with 0 if every test case passed or 1 if any failed. How Optics finds an element # For each value of an element, Optics tries the cheapest ways first. An XPath is looked up in the UI tree. Text is looked up in the UI tree, and if it isn't there, Optics reads a screenshot with OCR. A picture is matched against a screenshot. If everything fails and you've switched on AI self-heal , an AI model looks at the screen and tries to recover. How Optics finds elements covers the full order and how to tune it. h: Every way ends in plain text
d: Learn which way of creating tests fits your team. Every way produces the same files.
x: Optics gives you several ways to turn a user flow into a test. They all end in the same plain-text suite: CSV or YAML files that live in your repository and run with optics execute . You can mix them in one project, so a test someone recorded can sit next to one an AI agent wrote. Choose your approach # Write it No code List the steps in a spreadsheet or text editor. Anyone can read and review them. Record it No code Run steps one at a time against the live app in optics live . What works is saved. Describe it AI Type what you want in plain English. An AI model drives the app and keeps the steps. Delegate it AI Connect your AI agent with optics mcp . It explores the app and writes the suite. Code it in Python Code Call keywords from pytest or any Python script. Code it in Robot Framework Code Use Optics keywords in .robot files. Which one should I use? # We recommend recording for most people starting out. You see each step work on the real app before it's saved, and you end up with readable CSV files you can edit by hand later. Teams then usually write small changes directly in the files. Choose describe or delegate when you have an AI model key (Gemini, OpenAI, Claude) or an AI agent, and want a first draft of a long flow quickly. Review what the AI saved, the same way you'd review a colleague's change. Choose Python or Robot Framework only if your tests need logic that the files can't express, or your team already runs everything through pytest or Robot. Code-based tests lose the main benefit of Optics files: that anyone on the team can read them. d: Write test cases, modules and elements by hand, in CSV or YAML.
x: Writing a suite by hand is the most direct way to create tests, and it's how most edits happen once a suite exists. You need a text editor or a spreadsheet app. This page covers the three files a suite is made of, in the order we recommend writing them. Set up a project # Create a project with optics init , then fill in its files: $ optics init birch-tests Pick (Blank project) when asked for a template. You get this layout: birch-tests/ ├── config.yaml # what to drive ├── test_cases/test_cases.csv # which flows run ├── modules/modules.csv # the steps └── test_data/elements.csv # names for things on screen Optics finds each file by what's inside it, not by its name or folder. A CSV whose first row is test_case,test_step is a test-cases file wherever it sits. You can split a big suite across several files of each kind. If you haven't set up config.yaml yet, Install Optics and the platform guides show what to put in it. Choose CSV or YAML # Both formats load into the same suite, and one project can hold both. Pick the one your team reads best: CSV opens in any spreadsheet. Each step is one row, so a diff shows exactly which step changed. YAML keeps a whole flow in one indented file, which reads well in a code editor. The examples on this page show both. Choose a tab and the rest of the page follows. Write tests in YAML covers the YAML rules in detail. Name the things on screen # Start with elements : a name for each field, button or label your test touches, and how to find it. test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID email_field , //*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/email'] password_field , //*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/password'] sign_in , //*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login'] sign_in , Sign in search_bar , Search Birch password , correct-horse birch.yaml Elements : email_field : "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/email']" password_field : "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/password']" sign_in : [ "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']" , "Sign in" ] search_bar : Search Birch password : correct-horse The header is Element_Name,Element_ID , in any case. Repeat a name, or give a list in YAML, to add fallbacks : Optics tries the values in order until one works. Here sign_in is found by its id, or by its text if the id changes. A value can be an XPath, visible text, or the file name of a picture of the element. Define elements explains each kind and when to use it. Tip Elements can hold test data too, such as email,ava@birch.shop . Keeping data next to locators means one file holds everything that changes between environments. Each step is one keyword and its values. modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2 Launch Birch , Launch App Sign In , Enter Text , ${email_field} , ava@birch.shop Sign In , Enter Text , ${password_field} , ${password} Sign In , Press Element , ${sign_in} Sign In , Assert Presence , Picked for you Add To Cart , Press Element , ${search_bar} Add To Cart , Enter Text Direct , trail runner Add To Cart , Press Element , Trail Runner 2 Add To Cart , Press Element , Add to cart Add To Cart , Assert Presence , Added to cart birch.yaml Modules : - Launch Birch : - Launch App - Sign In : - Enter Text ${email_field} ava@birch.shop - Enter Text ${password_field} ${password} - Press Element ${sign_in} - Assert Presence "Picked for you" - Add To Cart : - Press Element ${search_bar} - Enter Text Direct "trail runner" - Press Element "Trail Runner 2" - Press Element "Add to cart" - Assert Presence "Added to cart" How a step is read: Keyword names are case-insensitive. d: Build a test by running steps one at a time against the live app, then save the ones that worked.
x: optics live opens an interactive session next to your device or browser. You type a step, Optics runs it straight away, and you see whether it worked. Every step that succeeds is recorded. When the flow is done, /save writes it into your suite as a module, ready for optics execute . Before you begin # You need a project with a working config.yaml that has exactly one driver enabled. Any project from optics quickstart or the first test tutorial works. For a phone, start the Appium server and your emulator first. See Android or iOS . Start a session # $ optics live birch-tests Leave out the folder to use the current one. Optics opens the app straight away (it runs launch_app for you), so the first line of the session is already a recorded step. The screen has three parts: ✓ launch_app 1.21s ✓ enter_text ${email_field} ava@birch.shop 0.48s [XPath] ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── › press_element "Sign in" ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── appium:emulator-5554 · rec ● · /help · /quit · Tab complete · Ctrl-K keywords · Ctrl-N AI mode History , at the top: each step with ✓ or ✗, how long it took, and how the element was found ( [XPath] , [Text] , [OCR] or [Image] ). Input , in the middle: where you type. Status bar , at the bottom: the device or browser you're connected to, and rec ● to show recording is on. Run steps # Type a keyword and its values, separated by spaces, and press Enter : › enter_text ${email_field} ava@birch.shop › enter_text ${password_field} "correct horse" › press_element "Sign in" › assert_presence "Picked for you" Write keyword names in snake_case or in words: press_element , Press Element and press element all work. Put quotes around a value that contains spaces. Type ${ to pick from the elements already defined in your project. Put a name inside a longer value, such as enter_text ${email_field} "ava+${tag}@birch.shop" . Live uses the first value of tag . A name that is not defined fails the step. Type name=value to give a parameter by name. For example, press_element "Add to cart" index=1 presses the second match. On Appium, index= also picks among native elements with the same text. Type go_back to go back one screen. Type assert_text ${greeting} "Hi, Ava" to fail the step when the element shows other text. Press Tab to complete a keyword name. The rest of its parameters appear in grey as a hint. Press Ctrl + K to browse every keyword. If a step fails, it's shown with ✗ and the reason, and it isn't recorded. Try a different value and run it again. Only steps that work end up in your test. Save the recording # When the flow works, save it with a test case name and a module name: › /save Checkout Sign_In • Saved 4 step(s) → module 'Sign_In' in modules/modules.csv, test case 'Checkout' in test_cases/test_cases.csv Optics then: appends the steps to modules/modules.csv as the module Sign_In , adds new elements to your elements CSV, or creates elements/elements.csv when the project has none, adds a Checkout,Sign_In row to test_cases/test_cases.csv , copies the session's screenshots to execution_output/Sign_In/ , clears the recording, so the next steps you run become the next module. Run more steps, then /save Checkout Add_To_Cart to add a second module to the same test case. Note Names in /save can't contain spaces. Use underscores, or rename the module in modules.csv afterwards. If the module or test case already exists, Optics asks you to run the same /save again to confirm that you want to append to it. /save writes the steps as you typed them. If you typed press_element "Sign in" , the module uses the text Sign in . To use a named element instead, type ${sign_in} , or edit modules.csv afterwards and add the element to elements.csv . /save always writes CSV, even in a project that uses YAML. /save does not write a value that you type into a secret field, such as a password. The step enter_text ${password_field} "correct horse" is saved as Enter T

t: Describe a test in plain English
h: Write goals the model can finish
d: Tell Optics what to do in a sentence, let an AI model drive the app, and keep the steps it took.
x: In plain-English mode, you type a goal like add trail runners to the cart . An AI model looks at the screen, picks one keyword at a time, and runs it on the real device until the goal is done. The steps it took are recorded like any other optics live steps, and /save writes them into your suite. It works with Gemini, Claude, OpenAI, or a model you run yourself. It's the fastest way to draft a long flow, and the result is ordinary keywords you can read and edit. Before you begin # You need: A project that works in optics live . An API key for an AI model, or a local model server such as Ollama. 1 Install the AI engine # Pick the engine for the account you have: You have Install A Gemini API key, or Google Cloud Vertex AI gemini An OpenAI or OpenRouter key, Azure OpenAI, or a local model in Ollama, vLLM or LM Studio openai A Claude API key, or Claude on Amazon Bedrock or Vertex AI anthropic Install that name, for example: $ optics setup --install gemini 2 Turn it on in config.yaml # Add an llm_models section to your project's config.yaml , using the same name: config.yaml llm_models : - gemini : enabled : true For a server such as OpenRouter or Ollama, add its url . Gemini uses gemini-2.5-flash unless you set a model . The other engines need one. Pick a model that accepts images, or set vision: never in Agent settings . See llm_models for every setting. 3 Give Optics your key # Set the engine's key in the terminal you run optics live from: $ export GEMINI_API_KEY="your-key" PS> $env:GEMINI_API_KEY = "your-key" Use GEMINI_API_KEY , OPENAI_API_KEY , ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , or the variable you named in api_key_env . A local server needs no key. You can also give the key in config.yaml , under capabilities.api_key . Optics uses it before the environment variable. Tip Write the key as a reference, such as api_key: ${GEMINI_API_KEY} . Optics reads the variable when it loads the file, so you can commit config.yaml with your tests and keep the key private. Describe a flow # Start optics live , then press Ctrl + N . The prompt changes from › to ai › . Type what you want in plain English: ai › add trail runners to the cart ⋯ [ai] add trail runners to the cart thinking: open search and look for the shoes ✓ press_element '//*[@resource-id="com.birch.shop:id/search"]' 0.42s [XPath] ✓ enter_text '//*[@resource-id="com.birch.shop:id/search_input"]' 'trail runner' 0.51s [XPath] thinking: Trail Runner 2 is the first result ✓ press_element '//android.widget.TextView[@text="Trail Runner 2"]' 0.88s [XPath] ✓ press_element '//*[@resource-id="com.birch.shop:id/add_to_cart"]' 0.37s [XPath] ✓ [ai] add trail runners to the cart done · 4 step(s) · 9.4s · recorded 4 (/save to keep) Each turn, the model sees the screen as rows, such as e7 button "Search Birch" [tap] #search . It also sees the last 8 steps, your project's element names and the keyword list. The model picks one action on a ref, such as e7 , and names the text that the next screen must show. Optics runs the action with a locator that matches only that element. Then it reads the screen again and judges the step as pass, fail or unknown. The model's thoughts appear as thinking: lines. Every action is a normal keyword, and the history shows the locator it used. Press Ctrl + X to stop a run, or Ctrl + N again to go back to typing keywords. You can mix both modes in one session. Keep the steps # The model ends a run with done and the text that proves the goal. Optics accepts done only when that text is on the screen. If the model gives no text, the run ends as PASS (unverified) . Check the app yourself before you keep those steps. When the run ends with done , Optics asks the model to remove dead ends and detours. Only the steps that mattered stay. Save the steps the same way as a manual recording: ai › /save Checkout Add_To_Cart Optics records only runs that end with done or PASS (unverified) . If the model gives up, reaches its step limit, or you stop it, Optics records nothing from that run. Review

t: Let your AI agent build tests
d: Connect Optics to Claude, Cursor or any MCP client so your agent can drive a device and write the suite.
x: optics mcp is a Model Context Protocol server. It gives an AI agent eyes and hands on a phone, TV or browser. The agent reads the screen as a list of rows, acts on a row by its reference, and sees what changed after each action. The agent explores your app, then writes an ordinary Optics suite that you review and run with optics execute . The agent is yours. Optics doesn't call any AI service in this mode, so it works with whichever model your client uses. Before you begin # An MCP client, such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor or VS Code. A target to drive: a browser (Playwright needs nothing else), or a phone or emulator with an Appium server running. See Platforms . 1 Install the MCP server # The installer includes the MCP server, so if you used it there is nothing to do. With pip, install the mcp extra in the same environment as Optics: $ pip install "optics-framework[mcp]" 2 Add Optics to your client # $ claude mcp add optics -- optics mcp Add this to claude_desktop_config.json ( Settings → Developer → Edit config ), then restart Claude Desktop: claude_desktop_config.json { "mcpServers" : { "optics" : { "command" : "optics" , "args" : [ "mcp" ] } } } Add this to .cursor/mcp.json in your project, or ~/.cursor/mcp.json for every project: .cursor/mcp.json { "mcpServers" : { "optics" : { "command" : "optics" , "args" : [ "mcp" ] } } } Add this to .vscode/mcp.json : .vscode/mcp.json { "servers" : { "optics" : { "type" : "stdio" , "command" : "optics" , "args" : [ "mcp" ] } } } If your client can't find optics , use its full path, for example ~/.optics/bin/optics . 3 Ask for a test # Describe the flow and where the app runs. The agent starts a session, explores, and writes files: Use the optics tools to open https://www.saucedemo.com in Playwright. Sign in as standard_user / secret_sauce, add the backpack to the cart, and check that the cart badge shows 1. Then write it as an Optics suite in ./checkout, run optics dry_run on it, and tell me how to run it. For a phone app, include the Appium details: start an appium session at http://127.0.0.1:4723 with platformName Android, deviceName emulator-5554, appPackage com.birch.shop . 4 Review and run the suite # The agent writes the same files you would: test cases, modules and elements, in CSV. Read them like a colleague's pull request, then run them: $ optics execute checkout What the agent can do # The server gives the agent: Session tools : start_session (picks the driver, URL and device settings, and opens the app) and terminate_session . Tools that act on the screen : tap , type_text , scroll , press_key , launch_app and check . observe lists the screen and can add a screenshot. run_keyword runs any other keyword, such as assert_text . Resources to read : the steps the session ran as CSV rows, the current screen, the raw UI tree and the keyword catalogue. optics://project-format teaches the agent how to write suite files. optics://browser-profiles lists the Chrome and Edge profiles on your machine. The screen comes back as rows such as e4 input "Login" [tap] #login-button . The agent taps e4 , and Optics uses a locator that matches only that element. Each action returns the rows that changed. When the agent adds the text it expects, such as expect_present: ["Products"] , the reply also gives a verified verdict. Optics waits up to 5 seconds for that text, so a page that loads late can still pass. A typical session goes: start a session, act on rows, check the result, read the steps and the project format, write the files, run optics dry_run , and end the session. The MCP reference lists every tool and resource. For one tool per keyword, start the server with --toolset full . Keep the agent on track # The agent asks you before it signs in. For a website that needs a sign-in, the agent reads optics://browser-profiles . It asks you which profile to use. If you choose none, it asks you for the credentials. Only a server that starts with the default stdio transport accepts a prof

h: How calls differ from suite files
d: Call Optics keywords from pytest or any Python script when a test needs real code.
x: Every keyword is also a method on the Optics class. Use it when a test needs logic the suite files can't express, or when your team already runs everything through pytest. You keep the same fallbacks, OCR and image matching as a CSV suite. Note If CSV or YAML files can express your test, prefer them. Anyone on the team can read and review a suite file, and the runner gives you the step tree, screenshots and error detection for free. See Choose how to create tests . Write a test with pytest # This test signs in to the Sauce Labs demo store, adds a backpack to the cart, and checks the cart badge and the price in the cart. It runs as written with pip install "optics-framework[playwright]" pytest . test_checkout.py import pytest from optics_framework import Optics CONFIG = { "driver_sources" : [{ "playwright" : { "enabled" : True }}], "elements_sources" : [ { "playwright_find_element" : { "enabled" : True }}, { "playwright_page_source" : { "enabled" : True }}, { "playwright_screenshot" : { "enabled" : True }}, ], } @pytest.fixture def optics(): with Optics(CONFIG) as session: # quits the browser when the test ends yield session def test_shopper_can_add_a_backpack(optics): optics.launch_app( "https://www.saucedemo.com" ) optics.enter_text( "//input[@id='user-name']" , "standard_user" ) optics.enter_text( "//input[@id='password']" , "secret_sauce" ) optics.press_element([ "//input[@id='login-button']" , "Login" ]) # fallbacks optics.assert_presence( "Products" , timeout= "10" ) price = optics.get_text( "//div[@data-test='inventory-item-price']" ) optics.press_element( "//button[@id='add-to-cart-sauce-labs-backpack']" ) optics.assert_text( "//span[@data-test='shopping-cart-badge']" , "1" ) optics.press_element( "//a[@data-test='shopping-cart-link']" ) optics.assert_text( "//div[@data-test='inventory-item-price']" , price) $ pytest test_checkout.py Configure the session # Pass the same lists you'd put in config.yaml , as a Python dict. driver_sources and elements_sources are required. The SDK reads these keys: Key What it's for driver_sources , elements_sources What to drive and how to look at the screen. See the config reference . text_detection , image_detection OCR and image matching engines, if you use them. project_path A folder to search for image files and to resolve relative paths in read_data . Required for image elements. execution_output_path Where screenshots and results go. To reuse a project's config.yaml , load it yourself and pass the dict: import yaml from optics_framework import Optics with open( "birch-tests/config.yaml" ) as f: config = yaml.safe_load(f) config[ "project_path" ] = "birch-tests" with Optics(config) as optics: optics.launch_app() Settings such as ai_self_heal , llm_models and log_level aren't read by the SDK. Test a desktop app # A desktop app uses the Appium driver with the OS and the app. See Test desktop apps for the setup: test_notes.py from optics_framework import Optics optics = Optics() optics.setup(config={ "driver_sources" : [{ "appium" : { "enabled" : True , "url" : "http://127.0.0.1:4723" , "capabilities" : { "platformName" : "Mac" , "automationName" : "Xa11y" , "app" : "com.apple.TextEdit" }}}], "elements_sources" : [{ "appium_find_element" : { "enabled" : True }}, { "appium_page_source" : { "enabled" : True }}, { "appium_screenshot" : { "enabled" : True }}], }) optics.launch_app() optics.enter_text( "//text_area" , "Hello from Optics" ) optics.assert_text( "//text_area" , "Hello from Optics" ) optics.press_keycode( "primary+a" ) optics.enter_text_using_keyboard( "<backspace>" ) optics.close_and_terminate_app() optics.quit() How calls differ from suite files # Method names are snake_case. Press Element is press_element . Your editor's autocomplete lists them all. Pass every value as a string. optics.press_by_coordinates("540", "1600") works; numbers raise TypeError . A list means "try these in order". press_element(["//button[@id='login']", "Login"]) tries the XPath, then the text. To che

h: How Optics keywords behave in Robot
Generate Robot code from a suite
d: Import Optics as a Robot Framework library and use its keywords in .robot files.
x: Optics is also a Robot Framework library. If your team already writes .robot suites, you can add Optics keywords to them and get its fallbacks, OCR and image matching without changing tools. Before you begin # Robot Framework isn't installed with Optics. Add it to the same environment: $ pip install robotframework "optics-framework[appium]" Swap appium for the engine you use. You also need a config.yaml with driver_sources and elements_sources . Any Optics project's config works. Write a suite # checkout.robot *** Settings *** Library OperatingSystem Library optics_framework.optics.Optics Suite Setup Open Optics Suite Teardown Quit *** Variables *** ${EMAIL_FIELD} //*[@resource-id="com.birch.shop:id/email"] *** Keywords *** Open Optics ${config} = Get File ${CURDIR} /config.yaml Setup config= ${config} *** Test Cases *** Shopper Can Sign In Launch App Detect And Press Allow timeout=5 Enter Text ${EMAIL_FIELD} ava@birch.shop ${sign_in} = Create List //*[@resource-id="com.birch.shop:id/login"] Sign in Press Element ${sign_in} Assert Presence Picked for you|Search Birch timeout=20 rule=any The suite reads config.yaml , so the same suite style works for a desktop app with a desktop config . On a desktop, Press Keycode takes a key combination such as primary+a . Run it like any Robot suite: $ robot checkout.robot How Optics keywords behave in Robot # Setup takes the config's contents, not its path. Read the file with Get File as shown above, then pass the text to Setup . If you use image elements, add project_path: . to the config so Optics can find the pictures. Pass fallbacks as a list. Create List builds the values to try in order. Writing several plain arguments fills the keyword's next parameters instead. Separate several elements with a pipe inside one argument: Picked for you|Search Birch . Named arguments use the Python names : timeout=20 , rule=any , index=1 . **There is no store_as .** Keep the return value in a Robot variable: ${price}= Get Text ${PRICE_LABEL} , then Assert Text ${CART_TOTAL} ${price} . Assert Text fails on different text. ** Go Back ** goes back one screen, and ** Is Element ** accepts the states checked and unchecked . **Robot replaces ${…} itself.** To pass an Optics variable to Evaluate or Condition , escape it: \${total} . ** Sleep and Evaluate exist in Robot's BuiltIn library too.** Robot warns and uses the Optics version, which only accepts whole seconds. Write BuiltIn.Sleep 2s or Optics.Sleep 2 to be explicit. The keyword reference lists every keyword. The Python-only keywords in Use Optics from Python , such as Add Element and Add Module , work in Robot too. Generate Robot code from a suite # If you already have a CSV or YAML suite, optics generate can write a starting .robot file from it. See Generate pytest or Robot code . See also # Use Optics from Python config.yaml reference

h: Open and close the app once
Run the same suite on different devices
Name things so failures explain themselves
d: Structure a growing suite with setup and teardown, shared modules, several files and run selection.
x: A handful of tests fits in three files. A suite that covers a whole app needs a little structure so changes stay small. This page covers the tools Optics gives you for that. Open and close the app once # Name a test case Suite Setup and it runs once, before every other test case. Suite Teardown runs once at the end. Use them to launch and close the app, so each test case can focus on its own flow: test_cases/test_cases.csv test_case,test_step Suite Setup , Launch Birch Shopper can sign in , Sign In Shopper can search , Sign In Shopper can search , Search For Shoes Suite Teardown , Close Birch modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1 Launch Birch , Launch App Close Birch , Close And Terminate App A name that ends with "Suite Setup" also works, such as Birch Suite Setup . Matching ignores case. Setup and teardown run even when you select which tests run . A test case whose name ends with Setup runs before each test case, and Teardown runs after each one. Use them to give each test a fresh start. If Suite Setup fails, the test cases do not run, and the report shows them as skipped. Suite Teardown still runs. If the per-test setup fails, only its test case is skipped. Tip Give each role to one test case only. Two test cases whose names end with "Setup" stop the run before it starts. A name such as Setup wizard works is an ordinary test case, because it does not end with "Setup". Reuse modules # A module can appear in as many test cases as you like. Keep each module small and focused on one screen or one task, such as Sign In , Search For Shoes or Open Cart . When that screen changes, you fix one module and every test that uses it follows. To call one module from inside another, use Execute Module : modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1 Buy Trail Runners , Execute Module , Search For Shoes Buy Trail Runners , Press Element , Trail Runner 2 Buy Trail Runners , Press Element , Add to cart Listing a module's name as a step on its own doesn't work; you need Execute Module . Steps inside a module called this way use only the first value of each element, so give important elements a value that's reliable on its own. Conditions and loops explains the details. Split a suite across files # Optics reads every CSV and YAML file in the project folder and its subfolders, and recognises each by its first row (or top-level key in YAML). So you can split a large suite however suits your team: birch-tests/ ├── config.yaml ├── checkout/ │ ├── test_cases.csv │ └── modules.csv ├── search/ │ ├── test_cases.csv │ └── modules.csv └── elements/ ├── shared.csv └── checkout.csv When two files define the same thing: Elements with the same name are merged, and every value becomes a fallback. Modules and test cases with the same name: the one read last wins, and Optics logs a warning. Keep names unique. Tip Optics also reads files inside execution_output/ . Keep stray CSV or YAML files, and copies of old suites, out of the project folder so they don't get picked up. Run only some test cases # Name the test cases to run, or to skip, on the command line. Wildcards * and ? work, and case does not matter: $ optics execute birch-tests --include "shopper can*" --exclude "Shopper can pay with a gift card" For a fixed selection, list the names in config.yaml instead. A flag replaces these lists for that run: config.yaml include : - Shopper can sign in - Shopper can search exclude : - Shopper can pay with a gift card Optics applies include first, then removes the exclude matches. Suite Setup and Suite Teardown always run. A name that matches no test case stops the run before it starts. Pick test cases gives the full rules. Run the same suite on different devices # Keep one config file in a project. Optics uses the config it finds in the project folder, so two of them would compete. To run the same suite on several targets, keep one config per target outside the project and copy the one you need into place before the run: birch/ ├── configs/ │ ├

h: A complete suite in one file
d: Keep a whole flow in one indented file, and learn the quoting rules that make YAML steps work.
x: YAML suites hold the same test cases, modules and elements as CSV, in one file you can read top to bottom. Optics loads both formats into the same suite, so a project can mix them. A complete suite in one file # checkout.yaml Test Cases : - Suite Setup : - Launch Birch - Shopper can add trail runners : - Sign In - Add To Cart Modules : - Launch Birch : - Launch App - Sign In : - Enter Text ${email_field} ava@birch.shop - Enter Text ${password_field} ${password} - Press Element ${sign_in} - Assert Presence "Picked for you" - Add To Cart : - Press Element "Trail Runner 2" - Press Element "Add to cart" - Assert Presence "Added to cart" timeout_str=10 Elements : email_field : "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/email']" password_field : "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/password']" sign_in : - "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']" - Sign in password : correct-horse Keep config.yaml as its own file. You can split the suite into several YAML files, or keep elements in CSV and steps in YAML. The rules # Section names are exact # Write the three top-level keys exactly as Test Cases , Modules and Elements , with that capitalization. Other spellings, such as test_cases: , are recognised as a suite file but load nothing, and the run then reports that there are no test cases. Each step is one line # A step is a single string: the keyword name, then its values separated by spaces. Optics matches the longest keyword name it knows at the start of the line, so Press Element Sign in is read as the keyword Press Element with the value Sign , then in as a second value. Quote any value that contains spaces: - Press Element "Sign in" - Enter Text ${email_field} "Ava Birch" A step that is exactly a module name runs that module. Named values # name=value sets one parameter by name, like timeout_str=10 above. Quote the value if it contains spaces: event_name="tap sign in" . A first value that starts with text= , css= or xpath= is a locator, not a named value: Enter Text text=Email ava@birch.shop . store_as=name keeps the value that the keyword returns: Get Text ${price_label} store_as=price . See Keep a value for later . Expressions with = in them # Quote an expression that contains spaces, the same as any other value. Optics removes the quotes: - Condition " ${status} == 'ready'" "Go Home" "Sign In" Module names as values # When a keyword takes a module name, such as Run Loop or Execute Module , quote names that contain spaces: Run Loop "Search One" ${term} "trail runner|pace knit" . Elements # An element is a single value or a list. A list gives fallbacks, tried in order: Elements : sign_in : [ "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']" , "Sign in" , sign_in.png] Quote XPaths. They contain characters YAML treats specially, such as [ , @ and : . What stays in CSV # Error definitions are CSV only. See Catch error screens . ** /save in optics live ** always writes CSV, even in a YAML project. Move the steps into your YAML file afterwards, or keep the CSV next to it. See also # Write a test suite , with CSV and YAML side by side Project files reference

h: 1. Each value of the element, in order
2. Each way to find that kind of value
3. Each element source, in config order
d: Learn how Optics tries several ways to find each element, so one changed locator doesn't fail a test.
x: Most test tools give an element one locator, and the test fails the moment that locator changes. Optics assumes an element has several identities (its place in the UI tree, its text, what it looks like) and tries them in order before giving up. A redesign that breaks one identity falls through to the next. The order Optics tries things # When a step needs an element, Optics works through three layers of fallback. 1. Each value of the element, in order # An element can have several values in elements.csv . Optics tries them top to bottom and stops at the first that works: test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID sign_in , //*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login'] sign_in , Sign in sign_in , sign_in.png 2. Each way to find that kind of value # Optics looks at a value and decides what kind it is, then tries the ways that fit, cheapest first: Value looks like Optics tries Needs An XPath, such as //*[@resource-id='login'] The UI tree A driver that exposes a UI tree Text, such as Sign in 1. The UI tree 2. OCR on a screenshot OCR needs a text detection engine An image file, such as sign_in.png Image matching on a screenshot An image detection engine CSS, such as css=#login The web page Playwright, or a web page on Appium. See Mobile web . text_only:Sign in OCR only, skipping the UI tree A text detection engine Looking something up in the UI tree takes milliseconds. OCR and image matching read a screenshot, which takes longer, so Optics only uses them when the tree can't help. Define elements shows every kind of value. 3. Each element source, in config order # config.yaml lists element sources : the ways Optics may look at the screen, such as asking the app directly, reading its UI tree, or taking a screenshot. For an action, Optics tries them in the order of the list, with each way that fits in each source. Assertions always try the UI tree sources before OCR and image matching. If you enable more than one driver, each is tried in turn as well. Last resort: AI self-heal # If everything above fails and you've switched it on, an AI model looks at the screen and tries to finish the step, for example by spotting that Sign in is now Log in . It's off by default. See AI self-heal . See which way worked # Optics records how it found each element, so you can tell when a test is passing on a fallback: optics live shows it after each step: 0.31s [Text] . When save_captures is true , screenshots in execution_output/ show a box around the element Optics found, for drivers that report element positions. See Read the results . If a test keeps passing on its second or third value, the first one is probably out of date. Update it while you still know why. Make elements last # Put the most stable value first. An id that developers don't change is better than text that marketing rewrites. Add a text fallback to important buttons. Text survives most layout changes. Use images last. Image matching is the slowest, and a restyled button stops matching. It's still the only option for icons with no text or id. Narrow the search when the same text appears twice on a screen. Use index to pick a match, or an area of interest to look in one part of the screen. See also # Define elements Find elements by text and image Search part of the screen AI self-heal

d: Name the things your tests touch, choose good values for them, and add fallbacks that survive redesigns.
x: An element is a name for something on screen, plus one or more values that tell Optics how to find it. Steps refer to elements by name ( ${sign_in} ), so when the app changes, you update the element once and every test follows. Write elements # Elements live in any CSV whose header starts with Element_Name,Element_ID , in any case. The project template puts them in test_data/elements.csv . test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID sign_in , //*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login'] sign_in , Sign in cart_icon , cart_icon.png search_bar , Search Birch email , ava@birch.shop To give an element several values, repeat its name on more rows. Optics tries them top to bottom. You can also add more columns whose names start with Element_ID , such as Element_ID_text or Element_ID_image , and fill them in on the same row: test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID,Element_ID_text,Element_ID_image sign_in , //*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login'] , Sign in , sign_in.png Both layouts mean the same thing. Use whichever is easier to read for your team. Empty cells are ignored. Choose the kind of value # Optics decides what a value is from how it looks: Write Optics treats it as Example Starts with / , // or ( XPath, looked up in the UI tree //*[@resource-id='login'] Plain words Text: UI tree first, then OCR on a screenshot Sign in text_only: then words Text, OCR only text_only:Sign in Ends in .png , .jpg , .jpeg or .bmp An image to match on a screenshot cart_icon.png css= , #id , .class or tag[attr] A CSS selector. Playwright and web pages on Appium only #login-button Starts with android. or XCUI A class name android.widget.Switch On Playwright, you can also write these prefixes. A prefix can be in any case: Write Finds id=login , data-testid=save , data-test=save , data-test-id=save An element by its id or test attribute testid=save The same as data-testid=save label=Email , placeholder=Search Birch A field by its label or placeholder alt=Birch logo , title=Open the cart An element by its alt text or title role=button[name="Save"] An element by its role and name text="Save" An element with exactly this text. text=Save also matches Save changes . loc=css:button.save , loc=role:button[name="Save"] , loc=href:/next The same as css= , role= and a link with this href . Agent browsers write locators in this form. See Locators for web pages . XPath # An XPath is a path through the app's UI tree. It's the fastest and most precise kind of value, and the best first choice when the app has stable ids: Android: //*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login'] iOS: //XCUIElementTypeButton[@name='Sign in'] Web: //button[@id='login'] To pick the second of several matches, wrap the XPath in parentheses and add an index: (//android.widget.Button)[2] . If the text isn't in the UI tree, for example because it's drawn inside an image or a game canvas, Optics reads the screenshot with OCR, as long as a text detection engine is enabled. Text matching in the UI tree tolerates small differences. To require exact matches, set strict_element_match: true in config.yaml . On Appium and Playwright, put text= in front to force text: text=(optional) . On Playwright, a value that looks like CSS, such as .com , is also tried as visible text. Put the picture anywhere in the project folder (the templates use test_data/input_templates/ ) and refer to it by file name only.
