t: Find elements by text and image
h: Enable it, and a screenshot source
d: Use OCR and image matching to find elements the UI tree can't see, such as text inside images, canvases and video.
x: Some things on screen never appear in the app's UI tree: text drawn inside an image, a game or map canvas, a video player's controls, or anything on a device you can only watch through a camera. Optics can find these by looking at a screenshot, the way a person would. It reads text with OCR (optical character recognition) and finds icons with image matching . Both are slower than the UI tree, so Optics only uses them after the faster ways fail. You turn them on in config.yaml . Turn on OCR # 1 Install an OCR engine # We recommend EasyOCR. It runs on your machine and needs no account. $ optics setup --install easyocr The first run downloads EasyOCR's models, which takes a minute. 2 Enable it, and a screenshot source # OCR reads screenshots, so elements_sources must include a screenshot source for your driver ( appium_screenshot , playwright_screenshot , selenium_screenshot , or camera_screenshot ): config.yaml elements_sources : - appium_find_element : enabled : true - appium_page_source : enabled : true - appium_screenshot : enabled : true text_detection : - easyocr : enabled : true 3 Use text values # Nothing changes in your tests. Any text value, such as Press Element,Trail Runner 2 , is tried in the UI tree first and with OCR second. To skip the UI tree and use OCR straight away, write text_only:Trail Runner 2 . Without an OCR engine, a text miss ends with "OCR was not tried: no text_detection engine is configured." OCR engines # Engine Name in config Install Good to know EasyOCR easyocr optics setup --install easyocr Local and accurate. Slower on the first call while models load. Reads English. Tesseract pytesseract optics setup --install pytesseract , plus the Tesseract program Light and fast. Matches whole words exactly. Google Cloud Vision google_vision optics setup --install google-vision Cloud service. Set capabilities.api_key to a Vision API key or capabilities.credentials_path to a service account key file, or set GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS . Screenshots leave your machine. Your own service remote_ocr Nothing Sends screenshots to a URL you run. See the engines reference . List more than one engine and Optics tries them in order. Pictures from a camera # The camera_screenshot source gives OCR and image matching a picture. The picture comes from one of three places: a webcam ( camera_index ), an HTTP(S) URL ( url , with an optional token ) or a TCP frame server ( url: ip:port ). See BLE and camera . Turn on image matching # Image matching finds a picture of an element, such as an icon, on the screen. It needs no extra install. config.yaml image_detection : - templatematch : enabled : true Then use the picture's file name as an element value: test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID cart_icon , //*[@content-desc='Cart'] cart_icon , cart_icon.png Capture a good template # The picture is called a template . How you crop it decides whether matching works: Take a screenshot on the same kind of device you test on. Run the test once and use a pre_… screenshot from execution_output/ , or run /screenshot in optics live . Crop tightly around the element. Include its distinctive shape, and as little background as possible. Don't resize the crop. Matching works best at the screen's own resolution, though it tolerates some scaling and rotation. Playwright screenshots are at CSS pixel scale, so crop Playwright templates from a Playwright run. Save it as PNG anywhere in the project folder. The templates use test_data/input_templates/ . Refer to it by file name only: cart_icon.png , not a path. File names must be unique across the project. Optics also picks up images inside execution_output/ . Give templates distinctive names, so they never clash with a screenshot's name. Before a tap, Optics changes the position of an OCR or image match from screenshot pixels to screen points, so that taps land correctly on iOS and on scaled screens. When to use which # Situation Use The element has a stable id or text in the UI tree XPath

d: Limit where Optics looks for an element, so repeated text can't be matched in the wrong place and vision runs faster.
x: An area of interest (AOI) is a rectangle on the screen. Give one to a step and Optics only accepts an element inside it. Use it when the same text appears in several places, such as an Add to cart button that also appears in a product description, or to make OCR faster by reading less of the screen. Set an area # Four values describe the rectangle, each as a percentage of the screen, from 0 to 100: Parameter Meaning Default aoi_x Left edge, from the left of the screen 0 aoi_y Top edge, from the top of the screen 0 aoi_width Width of the area 100 aoi_height Height of the area 100 The defaults cover the whole screen, which means "no area". Pass the values by name: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3 Add To Cart , Press Element , Add to cart , aoi_y=75 , aoi_height=25 This looks for Add to cart only in the bottom quarter: it starts 75% of the way down and covers the remaining 25%. Some common areas: Area Values Top half aoi_height=50 Bottom half aoi_y=50,aoi_height=50 Right third aoi_x=67,aoi_width=33 Centre aoi_x=25,aoi_y=25,aoi_width=50,aoi_height=50 The edges must stay on the screen: aoi_x plus aoi_width , and aoi_y plus aoi_height , can be at most 100. How it works # OCR and image matching crop the screenshot to the area before they search. They read less, so they're faster too. The UI tree can't be cropped. Optics finds the element as usual, then keeps it only if its centre is inside the area. This also applies to web pages on Appium. If the match is outside the area, Optics tries the next way, such as OCR. When save_captures is true , each step that uses an area saves a screenshot with the rectangle on it: …_with_aoi.jpg in execution_output/ . Use it to make sure that you chose the right part of the screen. Keywords that accept an area # Press Element , Enter Text , Enter Number , Clear Element Text , Get Text , Swipe From Element and Scroll From Element . Checks such as Assert Presence don't take an area. In the Python library, only press_element accepts area parameters. Area or index? # Both pick one match out of several. Use index when you know which match you want by order (the second Add to cart button). Use an area when you know where it is, which keeps working when items are added or reordered. You can combine them, but the order differs. For UI tree and web matches, index picks a match on the full screen first, and then the area is applied. OCR and image matching count index inside the area. See also # Find elements by text and image Define elements Action keywords

t: Recover failing steps with AI self-heal
h: Install the AI engine and set your key
Give the API key in config.yaml
How Optics points the model to the target
d: Let an AI model look at the screen and finish a step when every way of finding its element has failed.
x: AI self-heal is the last line of defence. When a step cannot find its element with any value or any method, Optics sends a screenshot to an AI model. The model then tries to complete the step. If the button now says Log in instead of Sign in , the model can find it and press it, and the test continues. Self-heal is off by default. When to use it # Self-heal keeps long runs alive through small, expected changes to the UI. Examples are a scheduled check of a production app, or a nightly regression. There, a full report is better than a stop at the first renamed button. Self-heal does not replace good elements. A healed step passes , so you must read the logs to see a real change in the app. Fix the element after the run, as Find out what healed shows. Turn it on # 1 Install the AI engine and set your key # Self-heal uses the same AI engine and key as plain-English mode . Install the engine and set its key, for example: $ optics setup --install gemini $ export GEMINI_API_KEY="your-key" 2 Enable it in config.yaml # config.yaml ai_self_heal : true llm_models : - gemini : enabled : true For OpenAI, Claude or your own model server, use the entry of that engine. See Choose a model . 3 Enable a screenshot source # The model works from a screenshot, so elements_sources must include a screenshot source, such as appium_screenshot or playwright_screenshot . Without one, self-heal does nothing. If the AI engine is not installed or the key is missing, Optics logs a warning and runs without self-heal. A run never fails because self-heal is not available. Choose a model # Self-heal works with each engine under llm_models . Use a model that accepts images. Model Engine Key Gemini gemini GEMINI_API_KEY OpenAI, or a hosted service such as OpenRouter openai OPENAI_API_KEY , or api_key Claude anthropic ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Your own server with an OpenAI-compatible API, such as vLLM, Ollama or LM Studio openai , with the server in url Only if the server asks for one Use your own model server # The openai engine can call any server with an OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. For example, a vLLM server can serve a small vision model on a machine in your network: $ vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct --port 8000 Set the server address in url and the model name in model : config.yaml ai_self_heal : true llm_models : - openai : enabled : true url : http://gpu-box:8000/v1 capabilities : model : Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct If you start the server with an API key, give the key to Optics as api_key: ${VLLM_API_KEY} under capabilities . If the server rejects JSON-schema output, set response_format: json_object . For a 2B model trained for self-heal, with measured results, read Self-heal broken locators with a 2B model on your own GPU . Give the API key in config.yaml # Each engine reads its API key from capabilities.api_key first, then from its environment variable. Write the key as a reference, so that the file stays safe to commit: config.yaml llm_models : - openai : enabled : true url : https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 capabilities : model : google/gemini-2.5-flash api_key : ${OPENROUTER_API_KEY} Optics reads the variable when it loads the file. If the variable is not set, the run stops before it starts. Logs and reports show **** in place of the key. The openai and anthropic engines also take api_key_env , the name of the variable to read. What it does # When a step that finds an element fails, Optics gives the model: The step that failed and the locator of its element. The name of the element in your suite, when the step uses ${name} . For Press Element,${stopwatch_tab} , the model gets stopwatch_tab . A screenshot and a list of the elements on the screen, each with a reference such as e7 that the model can name. Optics sends the UI tree only when that list is empty or does not show all the elements. Up to three rows of that list that are the closest match to the target, best first. See How Optics points the model to the target . The steps that ran befor

h: What happens when a step fails
d: Check a suite without a device, run it for real, and choose which test cases run.
x: Two commands cover almost every run. optics dry_run checks your files without touching a device. optics execute runs the suite on the device or browser in your config.yaml and writes the results to execution_output/ . Check the suite first # $ optics dry_run birch-tests A dry run reads every file and checks that: every test step names a module or keyword that exists, every keyword in every module exists, with a suggestion when you mistype one, every ${name} is defined in an elements file or by an earlier step, such as Evaluate , Read Data or store_as . This includes a ${name} inside a longer value. It does not tap, type or open anything, so it is quick and safe to run before every commit. It still starts the engines in your config.yaml , so they must be installed and a driver must be enabled. optics dry-run is the same command. A suite that uses only flow control keywords , such as Evaluate and Condition , needs no driver. optics execute follows the same rule. Run it # $ optics execute birch-tests Before the run, Optics checks that the target is reachable: for Appium, that the server answers and, for a local server on Android, that a device is connected; for Selenium, that the server answers. If not, it stops with a message saying what to start. Playwright needs no check. Then it runs Suite Setup , each test case in order, and Suite Teardown , and prints a live tree: Test Suite ├── Suite Setup | 1.21s | PASS │ └── Launch Birch | 1.21s | PASS ├── Shopper can sign in | 1.38s | PASS │ └── Sign In | 1.38s | PASS └── Shopper can add trail runners | 4.02s | FAIL ├── Sign In | 1.31s | PASS └── Add To Cart | 2.71s | FAIL ╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮ │ Total Test Cases: 3 | Passed : 2 | Failed: 1 │ ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯ What happens when a step fails # The rest of that test case is skipped, and its unrun steps show as NOT_RUN . The next test case runs as normal. One broken flow doesn't hide problems elsewhere. A Failure details box after the tree names each failed step and why it failed. Exit codes # Code Meaning 0 Every test case passed. 1 At least one test case failed, error detection found an on-screen error, or the run couldn't start (no driver enabled, server unreachable, missing files). 2 The command line is not valid, for example an unknown flag. 3 The test case selection is not valid. 130 You pressed Ctrl + C . 143 Optics received SIGTERM. CI systems use this to mark a build as passed or failed. Optics also writes the JUnit report when you stop a run with Ctrl + C or SIGTERM. See Read the results . Choose which test cases run # Name the test cases to run with --include , or the ones to skip with --exclude : $ optics execute birch-tests --include "shopper can*" --exclude "Shopper can check out" Matching ignores case. * and ? are wildcards. You can use both flags. Optics applies --include first. Suite Setup and Suite Teardown always stay in the run. A name that matches no test case stops the run before it starts, with exit code 3 . The message suggests the correct name. optics dry_run takes the same flags. To keep a selection for every run, put include and exclude in config.yaml . The flags replace them for one run. Options # Option What it does --no-use-printer Print plain log output instead of the live tree. Useful when a CI log viewer garbles the tree. --include NAME ... Run only these test cases. --exclude NAME ... Skip these test cases. --runner pytest Run the suite through pytest instead of Optics' own runner. Most projects don't need this. To skip the reachability check, for example when the server is behind a proxy the check can't see, set OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT=1 . How long steps wait # On Appium and Selenium, action keywords act on the screen as it is. They don't wait for it to change. On Playwright, an action waits up to 10 seconds for its element ( element_timeout_ms ). Checks wait: Keyword Waits up to Assert Presence , Assert Visibility , Validate Screen 3

d: Find out what happened in a run from the JUnit report, the screenshots and the logs.
x: Every run writes its results to execution_output/ inside the project folder. The terminal tree tells you what failed. The files tell you why . What a run writes # birch-tests/execution_output/ ├── junit_output.xml # pass/fail for every test, for CI ├── 2026-10-09T14-02-11-…-pre_press_element.jpg # the screen before each step ├── 2026-10-09T14-02-11-…-press_element_element_detection_result.jpg ├── 2026-10-09T14-02-14-…-failure_Shopper can sign in.jpg # the screen of a failed test case ├── 2026-10-09T14-02-14-…-failure_Shopper can sign in.xml # its UI tree ├── 2026-10-09T14-02-15-…-end_of_run.jpg # the last screen ├── page_sources_log.xml # the UI tree, captured during the run ├── failed_steps_elements.json # the elements on screen when a step failed ├── internal_logs.log # with file_log: true ├── execution_logs.log # with file_log: true └── logs.json # with json_log: true File When it's written Use it to junit_output.xml Every run Show results in CI. Standard JUnit XML that GitHub Actions, GitLab, Jenkins and others read. …pre_<keyword>.jpg Before each step that finds an element, with save_captures: true See what was on screen when the step started. …_detection_result.jpg When Optics found an element by position, with save_captures: true See exactly what Optics found, boxed in green. …_with_aoi.jpg When a step uses an area of interest , with save_captures: true Check the area covers the right part of the screen. It's drawn in blue. …failure_<test case>.jpg and .xml When a test case fails. Web pages write .html . See the screen and the UI tree where the test case ended. …end_of_run.jpg At the end of the run, before Suite Teardown See where the app was left. page_sources_log.xml or .html When the UI tree is read. Web pages go to .html . Find the right XPath or text for an element. failed_steps_elements.json When a step fails, with save_captures: true See each element on the screen of the failed step, with its label and bounds. internal_logs.log , execution_logs.log With file_log: true Read every attempt Optics made, including which ways of finding an element failed. logs.json With json_log: true Feed results into your own dashboards. detected_errors_<id>.json When an error screen was found See which error definition matched. Investigate a failure # Read the Failure details box in the terminal. It names the test case, the step and the reason. last error: gives the error of the last fallback value, and (cause: …) gives the root cause. **Open failed_steps_elements.json ** to see the elements on the screen when the step failed. On a web page, each element has a loc locator that you can copy into your elements file. **Open the failure_<test case> screenshot.** It shows where the test case ended. Then open the last pre_… screenshot before the failure. Is the screen what you expected? If it shows a loading spinner, the step ran too early: add an Assert Presence before it. If it shows a different screen, an earlier step went somewhere unexpected. Search the logs for the element's value. With file_log: true , execution_logs.log has a line for every attempt, such as Trying … on 'Sign in' ... FAIL . **Reproduce it in optics live .** Run the steps before the failure, then try the failing step with different values until one works. See Record a test . Turn on more logging # Add these to config.yaml : config.yaml file_log : true # write internal_logs.log and execution_logs.log json_log : true # write logs.json, a list of every run event log_level : DEBUG # more detail in the terminal and log files log_level takes DEBUG , INFO (the default), WARNING or ERROR . Use WARNING to keep the terminal quiet so the tree stands out. Read the JUnit report # junit_output.xml has one <testsuite> and one <testcase> for each test case. Suite Setup and Suite Teardown also have one. The suite name and each classname are the name of the project folder, so name the folder after the suite. Each <testcase> has kind , timestamp , time and status . A failed test case

h: What happens at the end of a run
d: Fail a run in CI when the app ends on a crash dialog, a "Session expired" message or any other error you define.
x: Some failures do not break a step. The app shows Session expired , or Android shows Birch has stopped , and the test still passes because no step looked for that message. Error detection catches these. You list the messages that mean something went wrong, and Optics checks the final screen for them in every run. 1 List the error messages # Create a CSV anywhere in the project. The template uses test_data/error_definitions.csv : test_data/error_definitions.csv error_code,match_string,description,severity ERR_CRASH , has stopped , The app crashed with a system dialog , critical ERR_NOT_RESPONDING , isn't responding , Android shows an ANR dialog , critical ERR_SESSION , Session expired , The user was signed out , high ERR_NETWORK , No internet connection , The app lost its connection , medium ERR_SERVER , Something went wrong , The server returned an error page , high Column Required What it's for error_code Yes A short name for the error. It appears in the report. match_string Yes Text that means this error is on screen. description No What the error means, for whoever reads the report. severity No Any label you like, such as critical or low . 2 Run the suite as usual # $ optics execute birch-tests There's nothing to switch on. If the project has an error definitions file, Optics uses it. What happens at the end of a run # Optics captures the screen once, reads all the text in the app's UI tree, and looks for each match_string . It does this before Suite Teardown when the suite has one, because a teardown often closes the app. Otherwise it does this after the last test case. Matching ignores case and finds the text anywhere: session expired matches Your session expired. Please sign in again. For each match, Optics: logs a warning, which you can read in execution_logs.log when file_log: true is set: ON-SCREEN ERROR DETECTED — code: ERR_SESSION | matched_on: match_string | match_string: 'Session expired' | severity: high | The user was signed out , adds a failing test case named on-screen-error-detection to junit_output.xml , after the other test cases, with one failure per match, writes the details to execution_output/detected_errors_<id>.json . The terminal tree shows on-screen-error-detection as FAIL and counts it in the summary: └── on-screen-error-detection | 0.00s | FAIL ╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮ │ Total Test Cases: 4 | Passed : 3 | Failed: 1 │ ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯ A detected error fails the run A detected error counts as a failed test case, so optics execute exits with code 1 . CI tools that read the exit code or the JUnit report show the run as failed, even when every step passed. See Run tests in CI . Write good match strings # Use a phrase only an error would show. has stopped is good. Error matches too much, such as a help page about error messages. Copy the exact words from a screenshot of the error, and keep them short. Matching is plain text, not a pattern, so * or .* are matched literally. Avoid text that appears in your own tests. A match anywhere on the last screen counts. Limits # The check runs once, on the last screen. If the app recovers before the run ends, the error isn't seen. Add an explicit check in your test for errors that can appear and disappear mid-flow, such as Assert Presence on the screen you expect next. It needs the app's UI tree. On production devices driven through a camera, there's no tree to read. Optics skips the check if the app is already closed when it reads the final screen. This happens when the last test case ran Close And Terminate App and the suite has no Suite Teardown. Close the app in Suite Teardown instead. Definitions are CSV only. optics dry_run , optics live , the HTTP API and MCP don't run the check. See also # Read the results Run tests in CI Project files reference

d: Run the same suite on every pull request and read the results in your CI system.
x: A suite earns its keep when it runs on every change. In CI, Optics needs the same three things as on your machine: Optics itself, the engines in your config.yaml , and something to drive. It reports through its exit code and a JUnit file, which every major CI system understands. Run a web suite # Web suites are the easiest to run in CI, because the browser runs on the CI machine itself. .github/workflows/optics.yml name : Optics on : [push, pull_request] permissions : contents : read checks : write # lets the report step post a check jobs : web : runs-on : ubuntu-latest steps : - uses : actions/checkout@v7 - uses : actions/setup-python@v7 with : python-version : "3.12" - name : Install Optics and the browser run : | pip install "optics-framework[playwright]==1.11.4" python -m playwright install --with-deps chromium - name : Run the suite run : optics execute birch-tests --no-use-printer - name : Publish results if : always() uses : mikepenz/action-junit-report@v6 with : report_paths : birch-tests/execution_output/junit_output.xml - name : Keep the run output if : failure() uses : actions/upload-artifact@v7 with : name : optics-output path : birch-tests/execution_output/ .gitlab-ci.yml optics-web : image : python:3.12-bookworm script : - pip install "optics-framework[playwright]==1.11.4" - python -m playwright install --with-deps chromium - optics execute birch-tests --no-use-printer artifacts : when : always paths : - birch-tests/execution_output/ reports : junit : birch-tests/execution_output/junit_output.xml CI machines have no display, so set headless: true under the Playwright capabilities in config.yaml : config.yaml driver_sources : - playwright : enabled : true capabilities : browser : chromium headless : true To use a browser grid instead of a local browser, set the Playwright url and keep the token in a CI secret. Then you do not need playwright install . See Use a remote browser . The permissions block lets the report step post its check. Without it, the step logs Resource not accessible by integration and no check appears. Pull requests from forks always get a read-only token, so on those the results are in the job log only. Run an Android suite # Android suites need an emulator and an Appium server on the CI machine. Linux runners with hardware acceleration, such as GitHub's ubuntu-latest , can run the Android emulator. .github/workflows/optics-android.yml name : Optics Android on : [pull_request] permissions : contents : read checks : write jobs : android : runs-on : ubuntu-latest steps : - uses : actions/checkout@v7 - name : Enable KVM run : | echo 'KERNEL=="kvm", GROUP="kvm", MODE="0666", OPTIONS+="static_node=kvm"' | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/99-kvm4all.rules sudo udevadm control --reload-rules sudo udevadm trigger --name-match=kvm - uses : actions/setup-python@v7 with : python-version : "3.12" - uses : actions/setup-node@v7 with : node-version : 22 - name : Install Optics and Appium run : | pip install "optics-framework[appium]==1.11.4" npm install -g appium appium driver install uiautomator2 - name : Run the suite on an emulator uses : reactivecircus/android-emulator-runner@v2 with : api-level : 34 arch : x86_64 script : | adb install app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk appium > appium.log 2>&1 & sleep 5 optics execute birch-tests --no-use-printer - name : Publish results if : always() uses : mikepenz/action-junit-report@v6 with : report_paths : birch-tests/execution_output/junit_output.xml Make sure deviceName in config.yaml matches the emulator ( emulator-5554 for the first one), and that appPackage and appActivity match the app you install. Decide pass or fail # optics execute exits with a non-zero code when a run does not pass, so the run step fails the job by itself: Code Meaning 0 Every test case passed. 1 A test case failed, or an error screen was found. The run also exits with 1 when it cannot start, for example when the server is not reachable. 2 The command line is not valid. 3 A name in --in

d: Use this checklist before you rely on a suite in CI or for production monitoring.
x: A suite that passes on your laptop can still be flaky, slow or hard to debug in CI. Work through these items before the team starts trusting its results. Your ticks are saved in this browser, so you can come back to the list. The suite # Every test case has a clear outcome in its name. Shopper can add a backpack tells whoever reads a failure what broke. Test 3 doesn't. Every screen change is followed by a check. On Appium and Selenium, action keywords do not wait. Put Assert Presence or Validate Element after any step that loads a new screen, instead of Sleep . See Run a suite . Important elements have a fallback. Give key buttons and fields a second value, usually their visible text, so one renamed id doesn't fail the run. See Define elements . No test relies on another. Each test case should be able to run on its own, with Suite Setup handling shared setup. Check with optics execute <folder> --include "<test case>" . ** optics dry_run passes.** Run it before every commit, and as the first CI step. The configuration # The Optics version is pinned in CI ( optics-framework==1.11.4 ). Upgrade on purpose, in its own change. Only the engines you use are enabled. Every enabled OCR or image engine loads at the start of each run, even when no step needs it. **No secrets are in config.yaml or the suite files.** Keep API keys in environment variables, and refer to them as api_key: ${GEMINI_API_KEY} . Keep passwords in CI secrets. The project folder holds one config file and no stray copies of old suites. Optics reads every CSV and YAML in the folder. The run # Error screens are defined. Add the crash, timeout and "something went wrong" messages your app can show to an error definitions file . CI reads the exit code and the JUnit report. An error screen gives exit code 1 and adds a failing test case to the report. See Run tests in CI . Screenshots are kept when a run fails. Upload execution_output/ as a CI artifact. File logs are on for CI runs. file_log: true gives you every locator attempt when a failure is hard to explain. Someone owns the failures. Decide who looks at a red run, and how fast. A suite people learn to ignore is worse than no suite. If you use AI features # Healed steps are reviewed. With AI self-heal on, a healed step passes. Search the logs for AI self-heal after each run and update the elements. Screens sent to the AI model are safe to share. Plain-English mode and self-heal send screenshots to your LLM provider.

d: Learn which platforms Optics drives, what each one needs, and which keywords behave differently.
x: Optics runs the same tests on phones, TVs, browsers, desktop apps and locked production devices. A driver controls the device, and element sources are the ways Optics looks at the screen. You pick both in config.yaml . Support matrix # Platform Driver Element sources Notes Android appium (UiAutomator2) appium_find_element , appium_page_source , appium_web , appium_screenshot Needs the Appium server, adb, and a phone or emulator. iOS appium (XCUITest) appium_find_element , appium_page_source , appium_web , appium_screenshot Needs a Mac with Xcode, and a simulator or a signed real device. Mobile web (Chrome, Safari, WebViews) appium appium_web with the Android or iOS sources Same setup as Android or iOS. Finds css= and DOM XPath locators in the page. Android TV appium (UiAutomator2) appium_find_element , appium_page_source , appium_screenshot Same setup as Android. Move around with D-pad key numbers. Samsung Tizen appium ( platformName: TizenTV ) appium_find_element , camera_screenshot Element keywords move the remote focus. Touch keywords fail with E0105. LG webOS appium ( platformName: LGTV ) appium_find_element , plus OCR Element keywords move the remote focus. Touch keywords fail with E0105. Web (Playwright) playwright playwright_find_element , playwright_page_source , playwright_screenshot No server. Opens Chromium, Firefox or WebKit on your machine, or connects to a remote browser. Can emulate a phone. Web (Selenium) selenium selenium_find_element , selenium_page_source , selenium_screenshot Needs a WebDriver server or Grid. Chrome or Firefox. Desktop (macOS, Linux, Windows) appium ( automationName: Xa11y ) appium_find_element , appium_page_source , appium_screenshot Needs Appium and appium-xa11y-driver on the computer that shows the app. Windows is experimental. Production devices (BLE + camera) ble camera_screenshot , plus OCR or image matching Taps through a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, and sees the screen through a camera. Enable one driver and the element sources whose names start with that driver's name. The config.yaml reference lists every key, and the engines reference lists what each engine installs. Choose a driver for web # We recommend Playwright for most people. It needs no server, optics setup installs its browser for you, and it runs on your own machine. Use Selenium when you already run a Selenium Grid, or need Firefox or a real Chrome on remote machines. It needs a WebDriver server running before each run. Test websites covers both. What changes between platforms # Between phones, browsers and desktop apps, only config.yaml changes. Your test cases, modules and keywords stay the same. To run a suite on another platform, copy the project and swap the driver and element sources. TVs on Samsung Tizen and LG webOS are the exception. They have no touch screen, so the element keywords press remote keys to move the focus. Touch keywords such as Swipe and Scroll fail with E0105 there. Use Press Keycode for single remote keys. Test TV apps shows the locators and key names. Element values usually do change, because each platform names things differently. Give an element one row per platform, and Optics tries each value in turn: test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID sign_in , //android.widget.Button[@text='Sign in'] sign_in , //XCUIElementTypeButton[@name='Sign in'] sign_in , Sign in The last row is plain text, which works on any platform with a UI tree, and with OCR on any platform that takes screenshots. Define elements explains fallback values. What doesn't work everywhere # Most keywords work on every platform. These are the exceptions: Keyword Where it differs Swipe, Scroll and other touch keywords Fail with E0105 on Samsung Tizen and LG webOS. Press Element and Enter Text move the remote focus instead. Press Keycode Takes Android key numbers on Android and Android TV, remote key names on Tizen and webOS, key names such as Enter on Playwright, and key combinations such as primary+s on a desktop. h: Install the Appium server and its Android driver
Start an emulator or connect a phone
Find the app's package and activity
d: Set up Appium and adb, then run your tests on an Android phone or emulator.
x: Optics drives Android apps through Appium , an open-source server that taps, types and reads the screen on a device. You run the Appium server on your machine, Optics talks to it, and Appium talks to the phone or emulator over adb (Android Debug Bridge, the SDK's device tool). This page uses Birch, a sample shoe store app with the package name com.birch.shop . Replace it with your own app. Before you begin # You need: Optics installed. See Install Optics . Node.js 20 or newer, to run the Appium server. The Android SDK. We recommend getting it with Android Studio , which also creates emulators. An emulator, or an Android phone and a USB cable. Set up # 1 Install the Appium engine # $ optics setup --install appium This adds the Python client that Optics uses to talk to Appium. It doesn't install the server. 2 Install the Appium server and its Android driver # $ npm install -g appium $ appium driver install uiautomator2 UiAutomator2 is the Appium driver for Android. It needs the ANDROID_HOME environment variable set to your SDK folder, and Java installed. Run appium driver doctor uiautomator2 to check both. 3 Make adb available # adb ships in the SDK's platform-tools folder. Add that folder to your PATH, then check it: $ adb version On macOS the SDK is usually in ~/Library/Android/sdk , on Linux in ~/Android/Sdk , and on Windows in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Android\Sdk . 4 Start an emulator or connect a phone # For an emulator, open Android Studio's Device Manager and start a virtual device. For a phone, turn on Developer options (tap Build number seven times in Settings > About phone ), then turn on USB debugging . Connect the cable and accept the "Allow USB debugging?" prompt on the phone. Check that adb sees it: $ adb devices List of devices attached emulator-5554 device The first column is the device's serial. device in the second column means it's ready. unauthorized means you still need to accept the prompt on the phone. 5 Find the app's package and activity # Optics needs the app's package (its id, such as com.birch.shop ) and its activity (the screen it opens on). Open the app on the device, then ask adb what has focus: $ adb shell dumpsys window | grep -E 'mCurrentFocus' mCurrentFocus=Window{4f2a1c u0 com.birch.shop/com.birch.shop.MainActivity} The part before the / is the package, and the part after it is the activity. If you know the package, you can also ask Android for its launch activity: $ adb shell cmd package resolve-activity --brief com.birch.shop priority=0 preferredOrder=0 match=0x108000 specificIndex=-1 isDefault=true com.birch.shop/.MainActivity An activity that starts with a dot is short for the package plus that name: .MainActivity means com.birch.shop.MainActivity . 6 Write config.yaml # Create a project with optics init birch-android , then replace its config.yaml : config.yaml driver_sources : - appium : enabled : true url : "http://127.0.0.1:4723" # where the Appium server listens capabilities : # must not be empty platformName : Android # required; picks the Android setup automationName : UiAutomator2 deviceName : emulator-5554 udid : emulator-5554 # optional; pins one device appPackage : com.birch.shop # app opened by "Launch App" with no value appActivity : com.birch.shop.MainActivity # appium:settings: {allowInvisibleElements: true} # optional; include off-screen elements elements_sources : - appium_find_element : {enabled: true} # asks Appium for XPaths, ids and text - appium_page_source : {enabled: true} # searches the app's UI tree - appium_web : {enabled: true} # finds css= and DOM XPath in web pages - appium_screenshot : {enabled: true} # screenshots for OCR and image matching text_detection : - easyocr : {enabled: true} # needs: optics setup --install easyocr image_detection : - templatematch : {enabled: true} # finds .png templates anywhere in the project log_level : INFO file_log : true json_log : true Always set url . Install the app and find its bundle id
d: Set up Appium with the XCUITest driver, then run your tests on an iOS simulator or device.
x: Optics drives iOS apps through Appium and its XCUITest driver, which uses Apple's own UI testing tools. You run the Appium server on a Mac, and Optics talks to it. iOS testing needs macOS, because Xcode only runs there. This page uses Birch, a sample shoe store app with the bundle id com.birch.shop . Replace it with your own app. Before you begin # You need: A Mac with Xcode installed from the App Store. Open it once to accept the license and install its components, then run xcode-select --install for the command-line tools. Optics installed. See Install Optics . Node.js 20 or newer, to run the Appium server. A build of your app: a .app for the simulator, or a signed build for a real device. Set up # 1 Install the Appium engine # $ optics setup --install appium 2 Install the Appium server and the XCUITest driver # $ npm install -g appium $ appium driver install xcuitest 3 Start a simulator # List the simulators Xcode provides: $ xcrun simctl list devices == Devices == -- iOS 17.5 -- iPhone 15 (5D1C2A60-8F0E-4B7A-9C41-2E6F0C3B9A17) (Shutdown) iPhone 15 Pro (A3E9F7B2-1C44-4D2B-8E0A-7B5D9C6E2F01) (Shutdown) Boot one by name and open the Simulator app to watch it: $ xcrun simctl boot "iPhone 15" $ open -a Simulator 4 Install the app and find its bundle id # Install your simulator build, then read its bundle id , the app's unique name: $ xcrun simctl install booted Birch.app $ plutil -extract CFBundleIdentifier raw Birch.app/Info.plist com.birch.shop 5 Write config.yaml # Create a project with optics init birch-ios , then replace its config.yaml : config.yaml driver_sources : - appium : enabled : true url : "http://127.0.0.1:4723" capabilities : platformName : iOS # picks the iOS setup automationName : XCUITest deviceName : "iPhone 15" # the simulator's name bundleId : com.birch.shop # required: the app Launch App opens # udid: <device udid> # real devices elements_sources : - appium_find_element : {enabled: true} - appium_page_source : {enabled: true} - appium_web : {enabled: true} # finds css= and DOM XPath in web pages - appium_screenshot : {enabled: true} If you have several iOS versions installed, add platformVersion: "17.5" so Appium picks the right simulator. 6 Check the setup # $ optics doctor birch-ios Without bundleId , the doctor shows a failure, because XCUITest has nothing to launch: Project ✅ config: driver appium enabled ✅ config: appium element source enabled: appium_find_element, appium_page_source, appium_screenshot, appium_web ❌ config: appium settings bundleId missing in capabilities → Edit config.yaml in this project folder. The adb rows in the Mobile section are for Android. Ignore them on iOS, even when the doctor lists the adb hint under "Before your first real run". 7 Start Appium and run # Start the server in a second terminal and leave it running: $ appium Then run the tests: $ optics execute birch-ios Before the run, Optics checks that the Appium server answers at url . Set OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT=1 to skip that check. The first session on a new simulator takes a few minutes, because Appium builds its helper app, WebDriverAgent, and installs it. Test on a real device # A real iPhone or iPad needs a few more steps: Connect the device, trust the Mac, and turn on Developer Mode in Settings > Privacy & Security . Find its id with xcrun xctrace list devices and set it as udid under capabilities . Sign WebDriverAgent with your Apple developer team, so it can be installed on the device. Signing is the step that most often goes wrong. Follow the Appium XCUITest driver docs for real-device setup. Write steps for iOS # iOS elements have types such as XCUIElementTypeButton and attributes such as name , label and value . d: Set up Playwright or Selenium, then run your tests in a browser.
x: Optics tests websites with one of two drivers. Playwright starts a browser on your machine and needs no server. Selenium sends commands to a WebDriver server, such as a Selenium Grid, which runs the browser. We recommend Playwright unless you already run a Selenium Grid, or need Firefox or a real Chrome on remote machines. The examples use the Sauce Labs demo store , which you can sign in to with standard_user / secret_sauce . Set up # Install the engine. Optics also downloads the Chromium browser that Playwright uses: $ optics setup --install playwright Then enable the driver and its three element sources: config.yaml driver_sources : - playwright : enabled : true # no url and no server needed capabilities : browser : chromium # or firefox, webkit headless : false # true: no window # viewport: {width: 1280, height: 800} elements_sources : - playwright_find_element : {enabled: true} - playwright_page_source : {enabled: true} - playwright_screenshot : {enabled: true} optics setup downloads only Chromium. For Firefox or WebKit, run python -m playwright install firefox or webkit in the Optics environment. There's no server to start, so optics execute skips its preflight check for Playwright. Chromium starts without the automation flags, so navigator.webdriver is false , as in a browser that a person opens. Selenium Chrome starts in the same way. Install the engine: $ optics setup --install selenium Selenium needs a WebDriver server. The quickest is Selenium's Docker image, which runs Chrome inside a container: $ docker run -d -p 4444:4444 selenium/standalone-chrome For Firefox, use selenium/standalone-firefox . If you already run a Selenium Grid, point url at it instead. Then enable the driver and its element sources: config.yaml driver_sources : - selenium : enabled : true url : "http://localhost:4444/wd/hub" # your Grid or standalone server capabilities : # must not be empty browserName : chrome # required: chrome or firefox browserURL : "https://www.saucedemo.com" # page opened when the browser starts elements_sources : - selenium_find_element : {enabled: true} - selenium_page_source : {enabled: true} - selenium_screenshot : {enabled: true} capabilities must include browserName , and only chrome and firefox work. optics configure writes capabilities: {} for Selenium, which can't start, so add these keys by hand. Other keys under capabilities are passed to the browser as WebDriver capabilities. Before each run, optics execute checks that the server answers at url . If it doesn't, Optics stops with a "Cannot start" panel. Set OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT=1 to skip the check. Then check the setup and run your tests: $ optics doctor my-web-tests $ optics execute my-web-tests Open the site # Launch App starts the browser. How it picks the page depends on the driver: Step Playwright Selenium Launch App,https://www.saucedemo.com Opens the browser at that URL. Opens the browser at that URL the first time. Launch App with no URL Opens a blank page. Opens browserURL , or a blank page if it isn't set. Launch Other App,https://www.saucedemo.com/cart.html Opens the URL in a new tab. Goes to the URL in the current tab. We recommend putting the URL in the Launch App step. Then the same module works with both drivers. Write steps for the web # Here is a full sign-in test for the Sauce Labs demo store. It works with both drivers: test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID username_field , //input[@id='user-name'] password_field , //input[@id='password'] login_button , //input[@id='login-button'] backpack_add_button , //button[@id='add-to-cart-sauce-labs-backpack'] modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2 Open the store , Launch App , https://www.saucedemo.com Open the store , Assert Presence , Swag Labs , 15 Sign in , Enter Text , ${username_field} , standard_user Sign in , Enter Text , ${password_field} , secret_sauce Sign in , Press Element , ${login_button} Sign in , Assert Presence , Products , 10 Add the backpack , Press E

h: Start Appium so that it can get chromedriver

d: Test web pages in Chrome, Safari and in-app WebViews on a real phone, in the same session as the native app.
x: Optics tests web pages on Android and iOS phones through the same Appium session that tests native apps. One test can open an app, follow a link into Chrome or Safari, fill a web form, and go back to the app. Your steps never switch contexts. To test a website in a desktop browser, or in a browser that only emulates a phone, use Playwright instead. This page is for real mobile browsers and WebViews. How it works # The session stays in the native context. Visible text, resource ids, native XPath and OCR work on web pages too. Chrome and Safari put the text, links and fields of the page into the native UI tree. Web locators, css=… and DOM XPath such as //button[@type='submit'] , go to the appium_web element source. It finds the element in the page in front, scrolls it into view, and gives its position on the screen. The tap or text entry that follows is a native action at that position. Before you begin # An Android or iOS setup that works: Appium, its driver, and a device or emulator. On Android, Chrome on the device. Set up # 1 Start Appium so that it can get chromedriver # Android web lookups need the chromedriver that matches the device's Chrome. Let Appium download it: $ appium server --allow-insecure uiautomator2:chromedriver_autodownload Or set appium:chromedriverExecutableDir to a folder of chromedriver binaries. iOS needs no extra driver. 2 Write config.yaml # Enable appium_web next to the other Appium sources. optics quickstart and optics configure do this for Android and iOS projects. config.yaml driver_sources : - appium : enabled : true url : "http://localhost:4723" capabilities : platformName : Android automationName : UiAutomator2 deviceName : emulator-5554 browserName : Chrome # start in Chrome; remove it to start in your app elements_sources : - appium_find_element : {enabled: true} - appium_page_source : {enabled: true} - appium_web : {enabled: true} - appium_screenshot : {enabled: true} With browserName: Chrome , the session starts in Chrome and web addresses open in Chrome, whatever the default browser is. To test an app that opens web pages, set appPackage and appActivity instead. config.yaml driver_sources : - appium : enabled : true url : "http://localhost:4723" capabilities : platformName : iOS automationName : XCUITest deviceName : "iPhone 17" bundleId : com.apple.mobilesafari # or your app's bundle id elements_sources : - appium_find_element : {enabled: true} - appium_page_source : {enabled: true} - appium_web : {enabled: true} - appium_screenshot : {enabled: true} Do not set browserName: Safari . It turns off the web lookups that appium_web uses. 3 Let Optics read the page # Chrome needs no setup. An app's WebView is readable only when the app calls WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true) . Debug builds usually do. Simulators need no setup. On a real device, turn on Web Inspector and Remote Automation in Settings > Apps > Safari > Advanced . Safari and in-app Safari sheets are always readable. An app's WKWebView is readable when the app sets isInspectable = true . 4 Run the sample # The mobile_web sample searches Wikipedia in Chrome on Android: $ optics init --name wiki --template mobile_web $ optics execute wiki Open web pages # Launch App and Launch Other App open a URL in the app that handles it. For a web address, that is a browser. modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1 Open shop , Launch App , https://shop.example.com/ Back to the app , Launch App , com.example.shop On iOS, Launch App opens the URL in Safari. Example: open a title from a grid
d: Drive Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS apps with remote-control keys and focus.
x: Optics tests TV apps through Appium , the same server it uses for phones. Each TV platform has its own Appium driver, and you pick it with platformName in config.yaml . On a TV you move around with remote-control keys and check what is on screen with assertions. On Tizen and webOS, the element keywords also work. They move the remote focus for you. TV platform platformName Appium driver How you move around Android TV Android UiAutomator2 Android key numbers, plus taps and typing Samsung Tizen TizenTV appium-tizen-tv-driver Remote key names, and element keywords that move focus LG webOS LGTV appium-lg-webos-driver Remote key names, and element keywords that move focus The examples use a TV app for Birch, a sample shoe store, with rows of shoes such as "Trail Runner 2" and "Pace Knit". Before you begin # You need Optics with the Appium engine and the Appium server: $ optics setup --install appium $ npm install -g appium Each TV also needs its own setup: developer mode on the TV, the vendor's tools, and the TV on the same network as your machine. Those steps belong to each Appium driver, and its project page covers them. Android TV # Android TV uses the same setup as an Android phone. Follow Test Android apps , with platformName: Android and the TV's serial from adb devices as udid . Connect to the TV with adb connect <tv-ip> when it is not on a cable. Touch and typing keywords work on Android TV, but most TV apps expect the D-pad. Send it with Press Keycode and Android key numbers: Remote button Number Up / Down / Left / Right 19 / 20 / 21 / 22 Select (center) 23 Back 4 Home 3 Play/pause 85 Remote key names such as UP do not work on Android TV. They only apply to Tizen and webOS. Samsung Tizen # Install the Tizen driver into Appium: $ appium driver install --source =npm appium-tizen-tv-driver Then configure Optics: config.yaml driver_sources : - appium : enabled : true url : "http://localhost:4723" capabilities : platformName : TizenTV appium:automationName: TizenTV appium:deviceAddress: 192.168.1.50 appium:rcToken: "14184553" appium:appPackage: com.birch.tv appium:app: /path/to/birch.wgt appium:chromedriverExecutableDir: /path/to/chromedrivers elements_sources : - appium_find_element : {enabled: true} Optics reads platformName and the app id ( appPackage , with or without the appium: prefix). It passes every other capability to the Tizen driver unchanged. The driver's README explains each one, including how to get the rcToken . A native screenshot makes a Tizen TV stop answering, so appium_screenshot refuses to take one there. To capture the screen, add the camera_screenshot element source. See BLE and camera for its settings. LG webOS # Install the webOS driver into Appium: $ appium driver install --source =npm appium-lg-webos-driver Then configure Optics: config.yaml driver_sources : - appium : enabled : true url : "http://localhost:4723" capabilities : platformName : LGTV appium:automationName: webOS appium:deviceHost: 192.168.1.50 appium:appId: com.birch.tv appium:rcMode: rc appium:useSecureWebsocket: true appium:newCommandTimeout: 600 elements_sources : - appium_find_element : {enabled: true} - appium_screenshot : {enabled: true} appium_find_element finds text in the app's DOM. Add an OCR engine ( optics setup --install easyocr ) to read text that the app draws as an image, or image matching for icons. The driver's README explains the capabilities. Check the setup # Start appium in another terminal, then run the doctor: $ optics doctor birch-tv The doctor's checks are written for phones. On Tizen and webOS it warns that deviceName , appPackage or appActivity is missing. You can ignore those warnings, and the adb rows, as long as config: driver and config: appium element source show ✅. Before each run, optics execute checks that the Appium server answers at url . It does not check the TV itself. Move around with remote keys # On Tizen and webOS, Press Keycode takes the name of a remote button: Key name Button UP , DOWN , LE

d: Test native desktop apps on macOS, Linux and Windows. Optics reads the accessibility tree of the OS through Appium.
x: Optics tests native desktop apps on macOS, Linux and Windows. It uses the same CSV files, keywords and reports as for phones and browsers. A test can open an editor, type a note, press a key combination, open a calculator and check a result. Note Windows support is experimental. It is tested on Windows Server 2022 with Notepad and the classic Calculator. Limits has the details for each OS. How it works # Optics talks to an Appium server. Appium uses appium-xa11y-driver , which reads the accessibility tree of the OS: the same data that a screen reader uses. Each button, field and menu item in the tree is an element that Optics can find, press and read. Appium and the driver run on the Host : the computer that shows the app. Optics can run on the Host too, or on a different computer that connects to the Host. Optics ──WebDriver──> Appium + appium-xa11y-driver ──accessibility API──> your app └───────────── on the Host ─────────────┘ OS Accessibility API Display macOS AXUIElement The desktop of the user that is logged in Linux AT-SPI2 An X11 display. The setup script starts one if there is none. Windows UI Automation The desktop of the user that is logged in Before you begin # Optics installed with the Appium engine: optics setup --install appium . A Host that runs macOS, Linux with X11 (Debian 13 is tested), or Windows (Windows Server 2022 is tested). On macOS, access to System Settings to give two permissions one time. On Windows, an administrator one time, if the Visual C++ runtime is not installed. The setup script installs its own Node.js, Appium 3 and the driver. You do not need Node.js before you start. Set up # 1 Set up the Host # Run the setup script on the Host. The script installs Appium and the driver, and starts Appium as a service on 127.0.0.1:4723 . It is safe to run the script again: it changes only what is missing. $ curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chinmayajha/appium-xa11y-driver/v0.1.2/hosts/mac/setup.sh $ bash setup.sh The service is the LaunchAgent appium-xa11y . Its log is ~/Library/Logs/appium-xa11y.log . $ curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chinmayajha/appium-xa11y-driver/v0.1.2/hosts/linux/setup.sh $ bash setup.sh The script installs Xvfb, Openbox, D-Bus and AT-SPI with apt . That step needs root: run the script as root, or with sudo access. If the script cannot get root, it prints the command to run yourself. The service is the systemd user unit appium-xa11y . It uses the X11 display that is there. If there is no display, it starts Xvfb on :99 . To see the log, run journalctl --user -u appium-xa11y . In PowerShell: PS> iwr https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chinmayajha/appium-xa11y-driver/v0.1.2/hosts/windows/setup.ps1 -OutFile setup.ps1 PS> powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File setup.ps1 The service is the logon task appium-xa11y of the user that runs the script. That user must stay logged on to the desktop. d: Test locked devices and live apps through a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard and a camera.
x: Optics can test a device with no automation software on it at all. A BLE dongle (a small USB Bluetooth adapter) pairs with the device as an ordinary Bluetooth mouse and keyboard. A camera pointed at the screen shows Optics what's there. Optics finds things in the camera picture with OCR and image matching, then moves the pointer and taps. When to use it # Use this setup when the usual drivers can't reach the device: USB debugging or developer mode isn't allowed , for example on locked company phones or retail devices. The app blocks screenshots , as banking and streaming apps often do. The camera sees the screen anyway. You monitor the live app. Synthetic monitoring runs the same journey on a real, unmodified device and app, the way a customer would. If you can use Appium or a browser driver, do. They're faster, read the UI tree directly, and support every keyword. What you need # A USB serial BLE HID dongle. It plugs into your machine as a serial port, and pairs with the device as a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard. A way to see the screen. Use one of these: a camera or capture card that your machine sees as a webcam, an HTTP(S) URL that returns a picture, or a TCP frame server. An OCR engine , such as EasyOCR, to read text in the camera picture. Image templates (optional), cropped pictures of icons that have no text. See Find elements by text and image . A stand that holds the camera square over the screen, so the picture doesn't shift between runs. Set up # 1 Install the engines # $ optics setup --install ble easyocr The ble engine adds serial-port support. The camera source and image matching need no extra install. 2 Pair the dongle with the device # Plug the dongle into your machine. On the device, open Bluetooth settings and pair with the dongle like any keyboard. A pointer appears on screen once it's connected. 3 Find the dongle's serial port # System Command Looks like macOS ls /dev/cu.usbmodem* /dev/cu.usbmodem1101 Linux ls /dev/ttyACM* /dev/ttyACM0 Windows Device Manager, under Ports (COM & LPT) COM3 Instead of a path, you can give the dongle's USB product description, such as MZ-BLE-VMK-001-v1.2.1 . Optics finds the matching port for you, which helps when the port number changes between reboots. 4 Point the camera at the screen # Mount the camera straight on, with the screen upright and filling the picture edge to edge. Optics turns positions in the camera picture straight into pointer moves, so anything around the screen throws the taps off. If the camera sees the screen at an angle, or sees more than the screen, set deskew_corners . Optics then cuts each frame to the screen and makes it straight. See camera_screenshot source . 5 Write config.yaml # config.yaml driver_sources : - ble : enabled : true capabilities : device_id : "Birch test phone" # a label for the device port : /dev/ttyACM0 # or the dongle's USB product description pixel_width : 1080 # size of the screen in the camera picture pixel_height : 2336 mickeys_width : 1080 # pointer units to cross the screen mickeys_height : 2336 x_invert : 1 # -1 if the pointer moves the wrong way y_invert : 1 elements_sources : - camera_screenshot : enabled : true capabilities : camera_index : 0 # or url: a screenshot URL, or "192.168.1.20:9000" for a frame server text_detection : - easyocr : {enabled: true} image_detection : - templatematch : {enabled: true} 6 Calibrate, then run # Follow Calibrate the pointer below, then start the app on the device by hand and run: $ optics execute birch-production There's no preflight for this setup, so check the dongle and camera before you start a long run. Settings # ble driver # Name Default What it does device_id Required A name for the device. port Required The dongle's serial port ( /dev/ttyACM0 , /dev/cu.usbmodem1101 , COM3 ), or its USB product description. pixel_width , pixel_height 0 The size of the device screen in camera-picture pixels. x: Most suites never need the features in this section. A list of modules with good elements and a few checks covers most user flows. Reach for these when a flow depends on data, needs to branch, or when another system needs to drive Optics. Logic and data # Variables Store values, compute new ones, and use them in later steps. Data-driven tests Run one flow once per row of a data file. Conditions and loops Branch on what's on screen, and repeat modules. Call APIs in a test Fetch or create data over HTTP mid-test, and use the response in later steps. Integrate # Run keywords over HTTP Drive a device from your own service with optics serve . Generate pytest or Robot code Turn a suite into code you can extend. Let your AI agent build tests Connect optics mcp to Claude, Cursor or any MCP client. Use Optics from Python Call keywords from your own scripts. How logic runs in a suite Flow-control keywords run other modules. Steps inside those modules work slightly differently from top-level steps: they use only the first value of each element, and they don't accept name=value parameters. Keep modules that run inside loops and conditions simple, and give their elements a reliable first value.

d: Store values, compute new ones during a run, and use them in later steps.
x: In Optics, a variable is an element that holds a value instead of a locator. You define some in your elements file, and some keywords create or change them while the test runs. Any step can then use the value with ${name} . Define a variable # Add a row to an elements file, like any element: test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID email , ava@birch.shop search_term , trail runner discount_code , WELCOME10 modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2 Search , Enter Text , ${search_bar} , ${search_term} Where ${name} works # You write Optics uses ${search_term} as the whole cell Each value in turn, the same as element fallbacks Hi ${first}! or ${first} ${last} The first value of each name. An unknown name fails the step. $${first} The text ${first} , not the value @:${password} The value, typed without @: and hidden in logs Evaluate , Condition , the query of Read Data and the URL, headers and body of Invoke API put in the first value themselves. Values are text shows how they quote it. optics live follows the same rules, so a name inside a longer value works in a recorded step too. Keep a value for later # Add store_as=<name> to a step to keep the value that its keyword returns. Later steps use the value as ${name} : test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID price_label , //*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/price'] cart_total , //*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/total'] modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2 Check Price , Get Text , ${price_label} , store_as=price Check Price , Press Element , Add to cart Check Price , Assert Text , ${cart_total} , ${price} Get Text reads the price and keeps it as price . Assert Text fails the step if the cart total shows different text. Any parameter column can hold the store_as= cell, but the column must have a param_N header. The keyword must return a value , as Get Text, Execute Script, Get App Version and Invoke API do. A keyword that returns nothing, such as Press Element, fails the step. Get Text returns no value when only OCR or an image found the element. A list or a dictionary is kept as JSON text. Only CSV and YAML suites read store_as . In Python and Robot Framework , use the return value. Create variables during a run # These keywords write a variable. Write its name as ${name} : Keyword Writes Example Evaluate The result of an expression Evaluate,${total},${price} + 5 Date Evaluate A date some days away Date Evaluate,${delivery_date},${order_date},+5 days Read Data A value from a CSV or JSON file, or an environment variable Read Data,${admin_email},test_data/users.csv,role == 'admin';select=email Invoke API Values from an API response See Call APIs in a test Run Loop The current item, once per pass See Data-driven tests modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3 Check Total , Evaluate , ${expected_total} , ${price} * 2 Check Total , Assert Presence , ${expected_total} Run Loop takes its count from a variable too: Run Loop,Add One Item,${n} . How long a value lasts # A value lasts for the whole run. A value set in one test case is available in later test cases and in Suite Teardown. A new value with the same name replaces the old one. Nothing carries over to the next run. Dry runs # optics dry_run defines each name that store_as , Evaluate , Read Data and Date Evaluate write. You do not need placeholder rows for them. Add a placeholder row only for these names: An extract name from Invoke API . A Run Loop variable that a top-level step uses. The dry run does not check the steps of the looped module. test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID access_token , placeholder Values are text # Every value is text, even when it looks like a number. That matters in expressions: Evaluate puts the value into the expression as you wrote it. ${price} + 5 with price set to 64 becomes 64 + 5 , which is 69 . To join text, quote it: '${first_name}' + ' ' + '${last_name}' . Read Data puts quotes around a value in its query,

d: Repeat one module for every value in a list, such as each user, search term or product.
x: A data-driven test runs the same flow several times with different inputs. In Optics, you write the flow once as a module, keep the inputs in a list, and use Run Loop to run the module once per item. Loop over a list of values # This example signs in to the Sauce Labs demo store as three different users, signing out after each one. It runs as written with the Playwright setup from Write your first test . test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID username_field , //input[@id='user-name'] password_field , //input[@id='password'] login_button , //input[@id='login-button'] menu_button , //button[@id='react-burger-menu-btn'] logout_link , //a[@id='logout_sidebar_link'] shoppers , standard_user|visual_user|problem_user modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3 Open the store , Launch App , https://www.saucedemo.com Sign In Each Shopper , Run Loop , Sign In And Out , ${username} , ${shoppers} Sign In And Out , Enter Text , ${username_field} , ${username} Sign In And Out , Enter Text , ${password_field} , secret_sauce Sign In And Out , Press Element , ${login_button} Sign In And Out , Assert Presence , Products Sign In And Out , Press Element , ${menu_button} Sign In And Out , Sleep , 1 Sign In And Out , Press Element , ${logout_link} Sign In And Out , Assert Presence , ${login_button} test_cases/test_cases.csv test_case,test_step Suite Setup , Open the store Every shopper can sign in , Sign In Each Shopper Run Loop,Sign In And Out,${username},${shoppers} reads: *run the module Sign In And Out once for each value in shoppers , and set username to that value each time.* Inside the module, ${username} is the current shopper. A few details make this work: **The loop sets ${username} .** You do not need an elements row for it. See Variables . **The values are separated by | .** You can also write them straight into the step: Run Loop,Sign In And Out,${username},standard_user|visual_user . ** Sleep,1 ** waits for the menu to slide open. Prefer a check such as Assert Presence to wait for a new screen, but use a short sleep for an animation on an element that's already on the page. The run shows the loop as one step. If any pass fails, the loop stops and the step fails with the reason: └── Every shopper can sign in | 7.26s | PASS └── Sign In Each Shopper | 7.26s | PASS └── Run Loop (Sign In And Out, ${username}, s... | 7.26s | PASS Loop over several lists at once # Give more name and list pairs to set several variables per pass. The lists are read side by side, and the loop stops at the end of the shortest: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3,param_4,param_5 Every Search , Run Loop , Search And Check , ${term} , trail|pace|ridge , ${expected} , Trail Runner 2|Pace Knit|Ridge GTX Search And Check , Press Element , ${search_bar} Search And Check , Enter Text Direct , ${term} Search And Check , Assert Presence , ${expected} Each pass sets term and expected from the same position in their lists: first trail and Trail Runner 2 , then pace and Pace Knit , and so on. Repeat a module a number of times # Give a count instead of lists: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2 Fill Cart , Run Loop , Add One Item , 3 Write the count as a number, or as a variable such as ${n} . Optics reads the value of the variable when the step runs. Keep the data in a file # Lists can live in an elements file, as shoppers does above, or as a JSON list: sizes,"[""8"",""9"",""10""]" . For a single value from a larger data file, such as the email address of the admin user, use Read Data : test_data/users.csv username,email,role ava , ava@birch.shop , admin ben , ben@birch.shop , shopper modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3 Sign In As Admin , Read Data , ${admin_email} , test_data/users.csv , role == 'admin';select=email Sign In As Admin , Enter Text , ${email_field} , ${admin_email} The query picks rows with a filter ( role == 'admin' ) and columns with select

h: Tap something only if it appears
Rules for modules run by these keywords
d: Run different modules depending on what's on screen or in a variable, and handle optional screens such as popups.
x: Most tests follow one path. Sometimes the app doesn't: a welcome popup appears only on first launch, a returning user skips sign-in, or a feature is behind a flag. Optics handles these with three keywords: Detect And Press for optional taps, Condition for branches, and Execute Module for running one module from another. Tap something only if it appears # For a popup that may or may not show, Detect And Press waits for the element and taps it if it appears. If it doesn't, the step still passes: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2 Launch Birch , Launch App Launch Birch , Detect And Press , Allow notifications , 5 Launch Birch , Detect And Press , Not now , 5 The second value is how many seconds to wait (30 by default). Keep it short: the step always waits the full time when the element never appears. Branch with Condition # Condition checks one or more conditions in order and runs the module paired with the first one that's true: Condition, <condition 1>, <module 1>, <condition 2>, <module 2>, …, <otherwise module> The last module, with no condition in front of it, runs when nothing matched. It's optional. Branch on what's on screen # A condition can be a module name . Optics runs that module: if it passes, the condition is true. Write a small module that checks for something, and use it as the test: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3 Is Signed In , Assert Presence , Picked for you , 5 Start Shopping , Condition , Is Signed In , Go To Search , Sign In If the home screen's Picked for you appears within 5 seconds, Optics runs Go To Search . Otherwise it runs Sign In . Put ! in front to flip a condition: Condition,!Is Signed In,Sign In . Warning The checking module really runs, so keep it to checks with short timeouts. A failed check waits its full timeout, and an action in it would change the app. Branch on a variable # A condition can also be an expression that compares variables: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3,param_4,param_5 Choose Flow , Condition , ${account_type} == 'business' , Business Checkout , ${account_type} == 'gift' , Gift Checkout , Standard Checkout Optics puts each variable's value in quotes before checking, so always compare with quoted text : ${account_type} == 'business' , ${count} == '3' . Compare numbers # Because values are compared as text, ${count} > 5 fails. Compute the comparison with Evaluate first, then check its result: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3 Check Cart , Evaluate , ${cart_is_big} , ${count} > 5 Check Cart , Condition , ${cart_is_big} == 'True' , Offer Free Shipping Evaluate puts values into the expression without quotes, so ${count} > 5 works there and stores True or False . Run one module from another # Execute Module runs a module's steps as part of another module: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1 Buy Trail Runners , Execute Module , Sign In Buy Trail Runners , Execute Module , Search For Shoes Buy Trail Runners , Press Element , Add to cart A module name written on its own as a step doesn't run that module. Use Execute Module . Rules for modules run by these keywords # Modules run by Condition , Execute Module and Run Loop follow simpler rules than top-level steps: Each element uses only its first value . Fallbacks don't apply. ** name=value parameters aren't available.** Give values in order: Assert Presence,Picked for you,5 , not timeout_str=5 . Their steps don't appear separately in the run tree. A failure message names the step that failed. If a branch needs fallbacks, give it its own test case instead and choose which test cases run with --include and --exclude . See also # Variables Data-driven tests Flow control keywords

d: Call an HTTP API in the middle of a test, check the response, and use values from it in later steps.
x: Some steps are faster or more reliable through an API than through the screen: creating a test account, fetching today's offer code, or checking that an order reached the backend. Invoke API calls an endpoint you describe in a YAML file, checks the response, and saves values from it as variables for later steps. The example on this page runs as written. It uses DummyJSON , a free public API for testing. 1 Describe the API # Create a YAML file anywhere in the project, with a top-level api: key. Group endpoints into collections , each with a base URL: test_data/api.yaml api : collections : dummyjson : name : "DummyJSON" base_url : "https://dummyjson.com" global_headers : content-type : "application/json" apis : login : name : "Sign in" endpoint : "/auth/login" request : method : POST body : username : " ${api_username} " password : " ${api_password} " expected_result : expected_status : 200 jsonpath_assertions : - path : $.accessToken condition : "len($) > 0" extract : access_token : $.accessToken me : name : "Who am I" endpoint : "/auth/me" request : method : GET headers : Authorization : "Bearer ${access_token} " expected_result : extract : email : $.email ** request ** sets the method, headers and a JSON body. ${name} is replaced anywhere in the endpoint, headers and body. ** expected_status ** is the HTTP status that the response must have. The step fails when the status is different, before Optics runs any other check or extracts any value. ** jsonpath_assertions ** checks the response. path picks a value, and condition is a small expression where $ stands for that value. A false condition fails the step. ** extract ** saves values from the response as variables, using JSONPath: $.accessToken , $.customer.id , $.items[0].name . 2 Add the inputs to your elements file # test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID api_username , emilys api_password , emilyspass access_token , placeholder email , placeholder The placeholder rows let optics dry_run accept variables that only get their value during the run. 3 Call the endpoints in a module # Refer to an endpoint as collection.name : modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1 Sign In Over The API , Invoke API , dummyjson.login Sign In Over The API , Invoke API , dummyjson.me Add a test case that runs the module: test_cases/test_cases.csv test_case,test_step API sign in works , Sign In Over The API The first call signs in and saves access_token . The second sends the token and saves the account's email . From here, any step can use ${email} : type it into a field, check it on screen, or compare it in a condition . A project with only API and other flow control steps needs no driver. Set every driver_sources entry in config.yaml to enabled: false . If a step uses an action, app or verification keyword, enable a driver. 4 Run it # $ optics execute api-demo └── API sign in works | 1.31s | PASS └── Sign In Over The API | 1.31s | PASS ├── Invoke API (dummyjson.login) | 0.66s | PASS └── Invoke API (dummyjson.me) | 0.64s | PASS Every request and response is logged to execution_output/api_details.log , and to api_details.har , which you can open in a browser's developer tools. Combine API and UI steps # A common pattern is to set up data through the API, then check it in the app: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2 Order Shows In App , Invoke API , birch.create_order Order Shows In App , Press Element , Orders Order Shows In App , Assert Presence , ${order_number} Creating the order through the API takes a second.
