d: Start a local Optics server and drive a device or browser from your own service, one keyword per request.
x: optics serve runs Optics as a small web server on your machine. Another program, such as an internal dashboard, a test orchestrator or a script in another language, can then open a session on a device and run keywords on it with plain HTTP requests. Each request runs one keyword and returns its result. Use the server when something other than Optics decides what to do next. If you want to run a suite, optics execute is simpler. If an AI agent is the caller, use MCP instead. 1 Start the server # $ optics serve It listens on http://127.0.0.1:8000 . Check it's up: $ curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/health {"status":"Optics Framework API is running","version":"1.11.4"} Use --port to change the port. Interactive API docs are at http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs while the server runs. 2 Start a session # A session is one connection to a device or browser. Send the same settings you'd put in config.yaml : $ curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/start \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "driver_sources": ["playwright"], "elements_sources": ["playwright_find_element", "playwright_page_source", "playwright_screenshot"] }' {"session_id":"23db1bdc-07d8-4cca-bfaa-1e9deaf4b794","driver_id":"PLAYWRIGHT_SESSION","status":"created"} Keep the session_id . Starting a session also opens the app, as Launch App would. For a phone, pass an Appium entry with its URL and capabilities: { "driver_sources" : [{ "appium" : { "url" : "http://127.0.0.1: 4723 " , "capabilities" : { "platformName" : "Android" , "automationName" : "UiAutomator2" , "deviceName" : "emulator-5554" , "appPackage" : "com.birch.shop" , "appActivity" : ".MainActivity" }}}], "elements_sources" : [ "appium_find_element" , "appium_page_source" , "appium_screenshot" ] } For a desktop app, give the OS and the app. See Test desktop apps : { "driver_sources" : [{ "appium" : { "enabled" : true , "url" : "http://127.0.0.1: 4723 " , "capabilities" : { "platformName" : "Mac" , "automationName" : "Xa11y" , "app" : "com.apple.TextEdit" }}}], "elements_sources" : [ "appium_find_element" , "appium_page_source" , "appium_screenshot" ] } 3 Run keywords # Send one keyword per request, with its values in order: $ curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/action \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"mode": "keyword", "keyword": "Launch Other App", "params": ["https://www.saucedemo.com"]}' {"execution_id":"ebbdc919-…","status":"SUCCESS","data":{"result":null}} $ curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/action \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"mode": "keyword", "keyword": "Assert Presence", "params": ["Accepted usernames are"]}' {"execution_id":"71f5ee34-…","status":"SUCCESS","data":{"result":true}} Keyword names work in any case: Assert Presence or assert_presence . params can also be an object of named values, such as {"element": "Login", "index": "1"} . A list inside it gives fallbacks: {"element": ["//input[@id='login-button']", "Login"]} . A keyword that fails returns an error status with the Optics code, for example 404 with E0201 for an element that is not found. See Errors . 4 Look at the screen # $ curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/screenshot \ | python3 -c 'import sys,json,base64; open("screen.png","wb").write(base64.b64decode(json.load(sys.stdin)["data"]["result"]))' /elements?compact=true lists the elements on screen. Each one has loc , a locator that matches only that element. /source returns the UI tree. 5 Stop the session # $ curl -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/stop {"status":"terminated"} This closes the app and ends the session. Follow a session live # Two endpoints stream updates as server-sent events : /v1/sessions/{id}/events sends a message when each keyword starts, passes or fails. /v1/sessions/{id}/workspace/stream sends a new screenshot and element list whenever the screen changes, which is handy for showing a live view of the device. $ curl -N http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/event

d: Turn a CSV or YAML suite into a pytest or Robot Framework file you can extend with code.
x: optics generate reads a suite and writes the same test as code: a pytest file or a Robot Framework file. Use it when a suite needs logic the files can't express, or when you're moving a suite into a codebase that already runs everything through pytest or Robot. The generated file is a starting point. Once you edit it, it no longer follows the suite files, so keep the suite as the source of truth for as long as you can. Generate a file # $ optics generate birch-tests Generated test file: birch-tests/generated/Tests/test_generated.py Generated requirements file: birch-tests/generated/requirements.txt For Robot Framework: $ optics generate birch-tests --framework robot --output checkout.robot Option Default What it does --framework pytest pytest or robot . --output test_generated.py or test_generated.robot The file name. It's always written to <project>/generated/Tests/ . The project needs a file named exactly config.yaml , plus test cases, modules and an elements file. What you get # Each module becomes a function (or Robot keyword), each test case becomes a test, and elements become a dictionary: generated/Tests/test_generated.py ELEMENTS = { 'username_field' : "//input[@id='user-name']" , 'login_button' : "//input[@id='login-button']" , } def sign_in(optics: Optics) -> None : optics.enter_text(ELEMENTS[ 'username_field' ], 'standard_user' ) optics.press_element(ELEMENTS[ 'login_button' ]) optics.assert_presence( 'Products' ) def test_shopper_can_add_a_backpack(optics): open_the_store(optics) sign_in(optics) Run it with pytest from the generated/Tests folder: $ pip install -r birch-tests/generated/requirements.txt $ cd birch-tests/generated/Tests $ pytest test_generated.py What isn't converted # Only the first value of each element is used. Fallbacks are dropped. Pass a list to keep them: optics.press_element([ELEMENTS['login_button'], 'Login']) . Flow-control keywords (Run Loop, Condition, Read Data, Evaluate, Invoke API and others) and a few more, such as Select Dropdown Option, aren't converted. Steps that use them are left out of the generated code silently. Check the output against your modules. ** store_as cells** are passed to the method as plain text, such as get_text(..., 'store_as=price') , which breaks the call. Use the return value instead. See Use Optics from Python . ** ${name} inside other text** is written as typed: 'Hi ${first}!' . **Every ${name} comes from the elements file.** A suite that sets values during the run, with Evaluate, Date Evaluate or store_as , runs as it is with optics execute . Suite Setup and Suite Teardown become ordinary tests. Image templates are copied only if they're in an input_templates/ folder at the project's top level. The runner ignores capitalization and collapses spaces, so Press Element , press element and press_element all reach the same keyword. If you misspell a name, the error suggests the closest match. Run optics list to print every keyword name in snake_case. Parameters # Parameters are positional. They fill the keyword's parameters in the order shown in each parameter table on these pages. To set a parameter by name, write name=value . This works only when name is a real parameter of that keyword. When a keyword's first parameter is element , its first text= , css= or xpath= value is the element, unless you also write element= . With pip, add it yourself: optics setup can't install it, and the all bundle doesn't include it. $ pip install "optics-framework[mcp]" The extra installs fastmcp 3.4.4 or newer. You also need the extras for your driver, for example appium or playwright . See Engines and extras . Start the server # optics mcp [--transport stdio|http] [--host HOST] [--port PORT] [--toolset core|full] Flag Default What it does --transport stdio stdio : your agent starts the server and talks to it directly. http : the server listens at http://<host>:<port>/mcp . --host 127.0.0.1 The address to listen on. http only. --port 8090 The port to listen on. http only. --toolset OPTICS_MCP_TOOLSET , else core core : the 10 tools below. full : also one tool for each keyword. See Full toolset . We recommend stdio for an agent on your own machine. Use http when the server runs in a container or on another machine. Over http , each session belongs to the client connection that started it. Another client cannot see the session or use its id. The server has no authentication, so keep it on 127.0.0.1 or behind a gateway that adds authentication. On another address, it logs a warning when it starts. Set OPTICS_ALLOWED_HOSTS to the host names that clients use, such as localhost in a container. A request with another Host is refused. An http server also refuses what makes it read its own files: project_path , credentials_path , file: URLs and Read Data from a file. Connect your agent # Most agents read a JSON file that lists MCP servers. For Claude Desktop it's claude_desktop_config.json ; for Claude Code it's .mcp.json in your project. Other agents use the same shape. .mcp.json { "mcpServers" : { "optics" : { "command" : "optics" , "args" : [ "mcp" ] } } } If your agent can't find optics , use the full path to it, for example /Users/ana/.optics/bin/optics . For the http transport, point the agent at the URL instead: .mcp.json { "mcpServers" : { "optics" : { "url" : "http://127.0.0.1: 8090 /mcp" } } } When the server runs in Docker and Appium runs on your machine, pass url: "http://host.docker.internal:4723" to start_session . Screen rows # The server shows the screen as rows. Each row has a ref, such as e7 , that the agent uses as a target: e2 input "Username" [tap,input] #user-name e4 input "Login" [tap] #login-button e6 h4 "Accepted usernames are:" The quoted text is on the screen. The #id is not. [...] lists what the element accepts: tap , long , toggle , input or scroll . A row without it is read-only text. A web row marked (off-screen) is on the page but scrolled out of view. A tap scrolls it into view. A ref stays valid while its element is on the screen. A ref from an earlier screen gives a stale_ref error. A tap on a ref uses a locator that matches only that element. The agent can also pass an exact label or a locator ( css= , xpath= , text= ) as the target. Core tools # The default toolset has 10 tools. Every tool except start_session takes session_id . You can leave it out when one session is open. When more than one session is open, the call fails with session_required and lists the ids. Tool Parameters (defaults) What it does start_session See start_session Starts a session. With app , it also opens the app or URL and returns the first screen. terminate_session none Ends the session and closes the driver. observe query (""), screenshot (false), max_rows (80, 1–300) Lists the rows. query keeps rows whose label or id holds the text. screenshot adds a JPEG of at most 1024 px. tap target , repeat (1, 1–20) Run

d: Learn the endpoints `optics serve` exposes for starting sessions, running keywords and streaming results.
x: optics serve runs a local HTTP server that lets any language or tool drive a device through Optics. You start a session, send keywords one at a time, and read screenshots, UI trees and events back. For a guided introduction, see Drive Optics over HTTP . The machine-readable OpenAPI document is at https://optics-framework.org/openapi.json . Start the server # optics serve [--host HOST] [--port PORT] [--workers N] Flag Default What it does --host 127.0.0.1 The address to listen on. --port 8000 The port to listen on. --workers 1 Server processes. Keep it at 1. Sessions live in each process's memory, so with more workers a request can reach a process that doesn't know your session and get a 404. The server prints its own log lines and Optics' debug logs to the terminal. Interactive docs are at http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs while it runs. Warning The API has no authentication. Anyone who can reach the port can control your devices. Keep the default 127.0.0.1 , or put the server behind a gateway that adds authentication. On another address, the server logs a warning when it starts. Two more checks keep web pages away from the server: CORS is off. A web page cannot call the server, unless you list its origin in OPTICS_CORS_ORIGINS , such as https://dash.example.com . Separate origins with commas. The value * stops the server with E0501. The Host header must be a loopback name. On 127.0.0.1 , a request with another Host , such as a domain that points to 127.0.0.1 , gets 421 Misdirected Request . To allow more names, or to apply the check on any address, list the names in OPTICS_ALLOWED_HOSTS . Separate names with commas. Loopback names stay allowed. In a container, publish the port on the host loopback and set OPTICS_ALLOWED_HOSTS=localhost : $ docker run -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 -e OPTICS_ALLOWED_HOSTS=localhost <image> The server does not read config.yaml or the test files of your project. Each session gets its engines from the request. Sessions do not save screenshots or page sources, and they log at DEBUG . Each session writes its other output, such as junit_output.xml , to its own temporary folder. The server deletes the folder when the session stops. Endpoints # Method Path What it does GET / or /health Checks the server is up. Returns {"status": "Optics Framework API is running", "version": "1.11.4"} . POST /v1/sessions/start Starts a session from a SessionConfig and launches the app. Returns {"session_id", "driver_id", "status": "created"} . POST /v1/sessions/{id}/action Runs one keyword from an ExecuteRequest . Returns {"execution_id", "status": "SUCCESS", "data"} . POST /v1/sessions/{id}/templates Uploads an image template: {"name", "image_base64"} . The image can be raw base64 or a data: URL. Use the name as an element for the rest of the session. Returns {"name", "status": "ok"} . POST /v1/sessions/{id}/api Replaces the session's API definitions for Invoke API . Send {"api": {"collections": ...}} . Returns 204. GET /v1/sessions/{id}/screenshot The current screen. data.result is a base64 PNG without a data: prefix, or "" if the capture failed. GET /v1/sessions/{id}/driver-id The driver's own session id in data.result . GET /v1/sessions/{id}/variables Every variable in the session: {"variables": {"name": ["value", ...]}} . GET /v1/sessions/{id}/elements Elements on screen in data.result . Query: filter_config ( all , interactive , buttons , inputs , images , text ; repeatable) and compact=true . compact ignores the filter. Appium, Appium web and Playwright only. See Compact elements . GET /v1/sessions/{id}/source The UI tree or HTML. data is {"page_source", "timestamp"} directly, not under result . GET /v1/sessions/{id}/screen_elements A screenshot and its elements from the same frame. data is {"screenshot", "elements"} directly, not under result . GET /v1/sessions/{id}/events A stream of keyword events. See Streams . GET /v1/sessions/{id}/workspace/stream A stream of screenshots and elements whenever the screen changes. See Stre

d: Learn what each Optics error code means and how to fix it.
x: When a step or command fails, Optics usually attaches a code such as E0201 . The code tells you which part of Optics failed, and the message after it says why. This page lists every code in Optics 1.11.4 and what to do about each one. How codes are built # A code is a letter followed by four digits. Part Meaning First letter E is an error. X is an error after Optics tried every fallback or caught an exception. W is a warning. First two digits The family: 01 driver, 02 elements, 03 screenshots, 04 keywords, 05 files and config, 06 engines and modules, 07 test cases and variables, 08 general, 09 optics live . Last two digits The specific problem in that family. Codes in the E02 family and X0201 mean "element not found". When a step uses an element with fallback values, only these codes make Optics try the next value. Any other code fails the step straight away. Where codes appear # Where What it looks like optics execute "Failure details" box <test> → step '<step>' — Keyword '<keyword>' failed: E0401: <message> , with (cause: <cause>) at the end when there is a deeper cause Log files ( file_log: true ) The same reason as the Failure details box, as an error line in execution_logs.log . A deeper cause follows as caused by: <cause> . Error panels A red panel with the code as its title. A deeper cause shows on a Caused by: line. optics live history ✗ press_element ${sign_in} with [E0201] ... on the line below HTTP API ( optics serve ) A code field in the error body, or the code inside a detail string. A cause field holds the deeper cause. See HTTP API . JUnit report ( junit_output.xml ) A code attribute on each <failure> , <error> and failed <kw> . See Read results . MCP server ( optics mcp ) [E0201] not found: ... in the tool reply, with a Next: line and the current screen rows. See MCP server . The cause is the innermost error of the chain, on one line of at most 300 characters. Optics leaves it out when the message already contains it. Not every failure has a code. See Messages without a code . E01: Driver and session # Code What happened What to do E0101 Driver not initialized. A keyword ran before the driver session started. In optics live this happens when the automatic launch_app failed. Start with Launch App . In optics live , run launch_app again and read its error first. E0102 Failed to start session. The driver couldn't create a session. The Appium server refused it, Playwright couldn't open or connect to the browser, or the request took too long. On Playwright, each call has a limit of action_timeout_ms (15 seconds). Launch App can take up to connect_timeout_ms + navigation_timeout_ms + action_timeout_ms (165 seconds). Check that the server is running and the device is connected with optics doctor <folder> . Check the capabilities, especially appPackage , appActivity or bundleId . Read the Appium server's own log for the cause. For a remote browser, check the url and headers . Raise the Playwright timeouts for slow pages. E0104 Driver config incomplete. A required driver setting is missing or wrong: empty Appium capabilities , no platformName , an unsupported platformName , or no server url . Also raised when Press Keycode gets a remote key name that a Samsung or LG TV does not know ( Unknown remote key '<name>' for <TV>. Known keys: ... ). The message lists the names that work. Also raised when Get App Version gets a name that is not an Android package name, such as com.example.app . Also raised when a desktop session has neither app nor appName ( A Mac session needs its app when it starts ). Fill in the driver settings in config.yaml . platformName must be Android , iOS , TizenTV , LGTV , Mac , Linux or Windows . On a desktop, set app or appName : see Desktop . For a TV key, use a name from Move around with remote keys . E0105 Keyword not supported on this device platform. You used a keyword on a Samsung or LG TV that needs a touch screen: a coordinate tap, a swipe, a scroll, Select Dropdown Option , the checked state

h: Ask a question or report a bug
d: Find the answer to a problem yourself, or report it so someone else can.
x: Most problems have a known fix. Start with the pages below, and ask on GitHub when they don't cover your case. Troubleshooting Fixes for common install, setup and run problems, listed by the message you see. FAQ Short answers about what Optics does, what it doesn't, and why. Glossary Every term the docs use, in one place. Where to look first # Run optics doctor on your project before anything else. It checks Python, every engine, the Appium server, connected devices and your config.yaml , and prints the fix next to each problem: $ optics doctor my-project Always pass the project folder. Without it, doctor checks your machine but not your config. If doctor shows no ❌ rows and the problem remains: **Search Troubleshooting for the exact message.** Problems are listed by the words Optics prints, such as No driver enabled or Element not found . Look up the code. If the message has a code like E0201 , Error codes says what it means and what to do. **Read the FAQ ** when something works differently from what you expected. Some behavior is a known limit, not a bug. Ask a question or report a bug # Open an issue on GitHub . Search the open and closed issues first, since someone may have hit the same problem. A good report lets someone reproduce the problem without asking you anything. Include: Your Optics version. Run optics --version . **The optics doctor output for your project.** Run optics doctor <project> and paste everything it prints. **Your config.yaml , without secrets.** Remove API keys, passwords and tokens, and replace private URLs with placeholders. The failing step. Paste the rows from modules/modules.csv and test_data/elements.csv that the step uses, and the full "Failure details" box from the run. The log. Choose the one that matches what you ran: optics execute : set file_log: true in config.yaml , run again, and attach execution_output/internal_logs.log and execution_output/execution_logs.log . Set log_level: DEBUG for the most detail. optics live : attach logs/optics_live_<time>.log from the project folder. Its path is printed when you quit. What you expected, and what happened instead. A screenshot from execution_output/ often shows the difference at a glance. Warning Logs and screenshots can contain personal data, such as names and email addresses on screen. Check them before you attach them to a public issue. Values written with the @: prefix are masked as **** in log files, but screenshots show whatever was on screen. Report a security issue # Don't open a public issue for a security problem. Report it privately, as described in the repository's security policy .

d: Fix the most common problems with installing, configuring and running Optics.
x: Problems are grouped by when they happen and named by the message Optics prints, so you can search this page for the words on your screen. Start with optics doctor <project> , which finds many of these for you. For messages with a code such as E0201 , see Error codes . Installing # optics: command not found # Your shell can't find the optics command. The installer adds it to your PATH, but only new terminals pick that up. Open a new terminal. If it still fails, add ~/.optics/bin to your PATH, as the installer printed. With pip, activate the virtual environment you installed into. Optics needs Python 3.12 or newer # Optics runs on Python 3.12 and later. pip on an older Python reports that no matching version of optics-framework exists. Check with python3 --version , then install a current Python from python.org or use the installer, which sets up its own environment. See Install Optics . "Cannot start": Optics could not load one of its dependencies # Every command stops with a red panel because a package Optics needs is missing or broken. This usually follows a partial upgrade or a package installed into the wrong environment. Run the reinstall command shown in the panel, for example pip install --force-reinstall optics-framework . It matches the way you installed Optics. optics setup refuses to install # optics setup and optics quickstart won't install engines into environments that another tool manages: Conda, pipx, uv tool , and project environments run by uv, Poetry, PDM or Pipenv. They also refuse a system Python marked as externally managed. Run the command the message suggests, such as pipx inject optics-framework … or poetry add … . Or install Optics into a plain virtual environment, where optics setup works. See Where installs are refused . EasyOCR fails under Conda # EasyOCR and Optics need different major versions of NumPy under Conda, so they can't share a Conda environment. Use the installer or a standard venv instead of Conda. The MCP server isn't installed by optics setup # optics setup --install mcp reports Invalid engine(s): mcp , and the all bundle leaves the MCP server out. The install scripts include it. With pip, install it yourself: pip install "optics-framework[mcp]" . See MCP server . Setting up a project # "Cannot start: E0104": No driver enabled in …/config.yaml # No entry under driver_sources has enabled: true , and the test cases use a keyword that needs a driver. Optics also prints this when it could not read config.yaml at all, for example because of a YAML syntax error or a value of the wrong type, and fell back to defaults. A suite that uses only flow control keywords needs no driver. Run optics doctor <project> . Its config: file row shows whether the file parses. Set enabled: true on one driver, or run optics configure <project> to write a working config. Check indentation: each engine is a list item, as in - appium: followed by its settings indented below. "Cannot start: E0501": Missing required files in …: test_cases, modules # Optics finds files by their header row, not their names, and found no test cases file or no modules file. Check the first line of each file: test_case,test_step for test cases and module_name,module_step,param_1,… for modules. Case does not matter. A spreadsheet app can add an invisible character to the first cell when it saves as "CSV UTF-8", so save as plain CSV. See How Optics finds your files . "Cannot start: E0102": No Appium server reachable at … # Before a run, optics execute checks that the Appium server answers at the url in config.yaml . Nothing is listening there. The report junit_output.xml shows each test case as ERROR with the same message. Start the server in another terminal with appium , then run again. For a desktop app, check that the Appium service of the Host runs: see Check that Appium runs . If the server runs on another port or machine, fix url under driver_sources . x: Short answers, with links to the pages that explain each one in full. These docs describe Optics 1.11.4. About Optics # Is Optics free and open source? # Yes. Optics is open source under the Apache 2.0 license, and the code is on GitHub . There's no paid edition, account or license key. Does Optics send my data anywhere? # No, not by default. Optics has no telemetry and needs no account. Tests, screenshots and results stay on your machine or CI runner. Data leaves your machine only through features you turn on: The AI features , plain-English mode and AI self-heal , send screenshots and the screen's UI tree to the provider you configure: Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, or the server in your url . A local model keeps them on your machine. Google Cloud Vision OCR sends screenshots to Google. EasyOCR and Tesseract run locally. Remote OCR and image engines ( remote_ocr , remote_oir ) send screenshots to the URL you configure. Event reporting sends the events you label with event_name to the eventUrl in your event_attributes_json file, if you set one up. With the MCP server , Optics itself calls no AI service. Your agent's client sends what it reads to whichever model it uses. What can I test, and where does it run? # Optics tests Android and iOS apps through Appium, websites through Playwright or Selenium, Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS apps through Appium, and native desktop apps on macOS, Linux and Windows through Appium and appium-xa11y-driver. It can also drive locked-down production devices as a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, with a camera watching the screen. Optics itself runs on macOS, Linux and Windows with Python 3.12 or newer. Testing iOS apps needs a Mac with Xcode. See Platforms . Can Optics test desktop apps? # Yes. Optics tests native apps on macOS, Linux and Windows through Appium and appium-xa11y-driver, which read the accessibility tree of the OS. You use the same CSV tests and keywords as for phones. Windows support is experimental. See Test desktop apps . Do I need to know how to code? # No. Tests are rows in CSV or YAML files: a keyword such as Press Element and the values it needs. You can record them by running steps against the live app, or write them in a spreadsheet. You'll edit a YAML settings file and use a terminal, but you won't write code. Python and Robot Framework are there if you want them. What is Optics not good for? # Optics tests what a person does through the interface. Use other tools for unit tests, load testing, API-only contract tests and pixel-by-pixel visual comparison. Creating tests # Should I use CSV or YAML? # Use CSV unless you have a reason not to. CSV opens in any spreadsheet app, and optics live saves recordings as CSV. Use YAML when you want a whole suite in one text file that reads well in code review. Both do the same things, and you can mix them in one project. Error definitions are CSV only. See Write tests in YAML . Can people who aren't developers write tests? # Yes. That's what the file format is for. A tester can record a flow in optics live and save it, then edit the CSV files in a spreadsheet. Someone comfortable with a terminal and YAML should set up config.yaml once; after that, most work happens in the CSV files. x: Terms are listed alphabetically. Each entry links to the page that explains it in full. A # Accessibility tree # The accessibility tree is the list of buttons, fields and texts that an operating system gives to screen readers. On a desktop, Optics reads it as the UI tree of the app. See Test desktop apps . AOI (area of interest) # An AOI, or area of interest, is a rectangle that limits where Optics looks for an element, given as percentages of the screen from 0 to 100. Use it when the same text or icon appears in several places. See Search part of the screen . Appium # Appium is the open-source automation server Optics uses to drive Android, iOS, TV and desktop apps. You run the Appium server yourself, and Optics connects to it at the url in config.yaml . See Drivers . appium-xa11y-driver # appium-xa11y-driver is the Appium driver that Optics uses for desktop apps on macOS, Linux and Windows. It runs on the Host with Appium. Set automationName: Xa11y to use it. See Test desktop apps . B # BLE driver # The BLE driver makes Optics act as a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, for devices that allow no automation software. A camera watches the screen, and Optics finds elements with OCR and image matching. See Production devices . Browser profile # A browser profile is the set of sign-ins, cookies and settings that Chrome or Edge keeps for one person. Set profile in the Playwright capabilities, and Optics starts the browser with a temporary copy of it. See Start signed in with a browser profile . C # Capabilities # Capabilities are the settings Optics passes to a driver when it starts a session, such as the device name, the app to open or the browser to use. They go under capabilities for each driver in config.yaml . See driver_sources . Chord # A chord is a key combination, such as cmd+s or ctrl+shift+t . On a desktop, Press Keycode takes a chord. primary is Cmd on macOS and Ctrl on Linux and Windows. See Press keys and key combinations . config.yaml # config.yaml is the settings file in each project. It says which driver to use, how to look at the screen, and how to log and report. See config.yaml . CSV # CSV (comma-separated values) is the plain-text table format most Optics suites use, one row per step. Any spreadsheet app or text editor can open it. See Choose CSV or YAML . D # Driver # A driver is the engine that controls the target: Appium for phones, TVs and desktop apps, Playwright or Selenium for browsers, or the BLE driver for locked-down devices. You enable one under driver_sources in config.yaml . See Drivers . Dry run # A dry run, started with optics dry_run , checks a project for unknown keywords, missing modules and undefined variables without tapping or typing anything. Run one before every commit. See optics dry_run . E # Element # An element is a name for something on screen, such as sign_in , plus one or more values that tell Optics how to find it. Steps refer to it as ${sign_in} . See Define elements . Element source # An element source is a way for Optics to look at the screen: ask the app for an element, read its UI tree, or take a screenshot. Each driver has its own, listed under elements_sources in config.yaml . See Element sources . Elements file # An elements file is a CSV whose header is Element_Name,Element_ID , in any case, listing each element's name and values. The project template keeps it in test_data/elements.csv . See Elements . Engine # An engine is an optional add-on that gives Optics a capability: a driver, an element source, an OCR engine, image matching or an AI model. You install engines with optics setup and turn them on in config.yaml . See Engines and extras . Error definition # An error definition is a row in a CSV that names a message your app shows when something goes wrong, such as "Something went wrong". At the end of a run, Optics checks the last screen for these messages and reports any it finds. See Catch error screens . Execution output # The execution output is the execution_output/
